articles.title_orig: Pope Leo leaves hospital after lung cancer operation
articles.title_zh: Pope Leo leaves hospital after lung cancer operation
articles.content_orig:
The surgeon who operated on Pope Leo XIV earlier this week detailed in an interview with Vatican News how the pope's cancer was discovered, moments before and after his surgical procedure and the importance of prevention.
The pope was discharged from the hospital Saturday — four days after his surgery — to a large crowd of well-wishers cheering for him.
Dr. Stefano Margaritora, director of the thoracic surgery unit at the Agostino Gemelli University Hospital Foundation, spoke to the Vatican News in a lengthy interview and said the pope's lung cancer was discovered "entirely by chance."
"The Holy Father falls into the category of people who discover they have lung cancer entirely by chance — not because they are undergoing preventive screening, but because they undergo examinations for other reasons," Margaritora said.
Margaritora said the tumor was found at the base of the right lung, but if it had been "a little higher up, it certainly would not have been seen."
Unfortunately, the doctor said, in its early stages, cancers can show no symptoms — such as the lung cancer the pope was diagnosed with. That's why regular preventive checkups for other cancers are so important, he said.
"He had no respiratory symptoms and felt perfectly well," said Margaritora.
The 71-year-old pontiff revealed the news at the end of his Sunday noon blessing last week before thousands of people in St. Peter's Square.
Margaritora said the operation to remove a lung nodule was routine and went forward "without any complications." The pope was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma , a common cancer, during the surgery.
The doctor said that for the four days the pope recovered at Rome's Gemelli Hospital, he was "an ideal patient."
"I am not saying that to flatter him. He truly did not cause the slightest problem for the team caring for him ... ," the doctor told Vatican News.
He said on the second day following the surgery, medical staff found the pope arranging the chairs in the hospital's makeshift chapel. Margaritora recounted that staff offered to move the chairs, "Holy Father, we can do that." And he replied, "It doesn't matter. I can do it, so I will."
The pope had already resumed some work activity on Thursday. By Friday, the pope had spoken with Russian President Vladimir Putin over the phone. Pictures of the American-born pope standing at an altar in green vestments, celebrating Mass at a small hospital chapel, were released by the Vatican.
He also held separate meetings with Cardinal Luis Antonio Tagle, the dean of the College of Cardinals, and Cardinal Baldassare Reina, the vicar general of the Diocese of Rome. The pope is scheduled to travel Nov. 6-17 to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru.

Emmanuel Macron has said there is “no room for violence” after hundreds of thousands took to the streets to protest France’s cost of living crisis on Saturday.
“Those who have broken, attacked the prefectures as well as businesses, looted even our town halls, will be prosecuted and punished,” the French president said.
Around 400 people were arrested on Saturday, interior minister Laurent Nunez told French media in a briefing. The government says around 550,000 protesters took part across the country, with organisers estimating the number at 800,000.
The interior ministry saying there had been violent incidents involving hooded individuals in Paris, Marseille, Rennes, Toulouse and Angers.
A large police presence was visible in central Paris, especially near landmarks such as the Avenue des Champs-Elysees and the Arc de Triomphe, with police firing tear gas at protesters who had climbed on monuments.
Protesters chanted about a repeat of the French Revolution, declaring: “It's the Revolution − we're taking the Bastille!" as they stormed the mayor’s offices in Marseille, according to Le Monde .
The protests began last ‌month at high schools in Paris' poor northern suburbs, where anger over teacher absences and shabby facilities quickly morphed into a nationwide movement against inequality, weak public spending and falling standards.
As demonstrations explode across France on Saturday, hundreds of people will head to petrol stations, oil depots, and refineries to protest.
The nationwide movement is part of a revolt against growing inequalities, including rising fuel prices and the cost of living.
Yellow Vests, one of the organisations leading today's protests, said 384 protests will take place at petrol stations in France, 38 at oil depots and five at refineries.
It said: “The gross refining margin has multiplied by 4.4 between the 2025 average and August 2026. It is 8.4 times higher than in May 2017, at the time of Emmanuel Macron's election.
“Over the same period, the distribution margin of the stations remained stable: 28.1 cents per litre of diesel before the crisis, 26.7 cents between March and May 2026.
“The action takes place in front of the pumps, where the price is displayed, and upstream: in front of the refineries, where the margin has been multiplied, and in front of the oil depots that supply the stations.”
A 19-year-old protester in Paris name Lola said: “We are fighting because the cost of living is too harsh, because the price of fuel is too high, because high school pupils are being violently attacked and hurt all over the country just for trying to protest and ask for more teachers and decent learning conditions.”
We’ve heard again from French president Emmanuel Macron who has said there is “no room for violence” after hundreds of thousands took to the streets to protest France’s cost of living crisis on Saturday.
“Those who have broken, attacked the prefectures as well as businesses, looted even our town halls, will be prosecuted and punished,” the French president said.
He expressed his support for law enforcement against the “sowers of chaos” who seek to “bring down our institutions”.
Around 400 people have been arrested in Saturday’s widespread protests, Laurent Nunez, France’s Minister of the Interior has said.
Mr Nunez was speaking to French media after a day which has seen major clashes between demonstrators and police across the country.
His ministry says around 550,000 demonstrators participated in France, while organisers said there were around 800,000.
The protests in France began last ‌month at high schools in Paris' poor northern suburbs, where anger over teacher shortages and shabby facilities evolved into a broader movement focused on inequality, public spending and living standards.
But they have now spread into a widespread display of discontent over the cost of living in France.
Police tactics have drawn criticism following injuries among demonstrators, including a teenager who lost a hand after picking up a stun grenade.
Lecornu said more than 900 police officers had also been injured in previous protests.
The police watchdog is investigating at least two dozen allegations of police violence.
In protests partly inspired by those in France, several hundred mostly young people protested in Brussels, and some clashed with police.
Belgian student groups have said they are protesting against rising education costs and reforms they fear will make higher education less accessible.
In Albania, police fired what appeared to be rubber bullets at protesters during a fifth day of mass student demonstrations calling for Prime Minister Edi Rama to step down.
In Portugal, tens of thousands took to the streets of Lisbon following days of unrest to protest against housing and other living costs. Housing prices in Portugal have doubled since 2017, fuelling one of the worst affordability crises in Europe.
In Italy, a march against high costs of living in Milan degenerated into disorder, with police clearing the central Cathedral square with tear gas.
Police in Bologna used water cannon to try to disperse crowds and made seven arrests after another protest turned violent, the ANSA news agency reported.
Clashes have broken out between police and protesters in cities across France as tens of thousands of people angered by rising costs and declining public services took to the streets – in some of the country's most violent protests of recent times.
More than 270 people have been arrested across the country, while in Lyon, protesters torched the tourist office. In Marseille, the mayor said the town hall had been vandalised and that additional police were being sent to the city following talks with the government.
The protesters said most people were protesting peacefully and put much of the violence down to troublemakers who had set out to cause damage and clash with the police. The Interior Ministry said, however, that violence was increasing, and that there had been "confrontations with law enforcement, looting or attempted looting of shops, attacks on and damage to public buildings." It blamed the unrest on ⁠what it described as the "ultra-left".
Holly Evans brings the full report:
French protesters have chanted that another revolution is underway, with hundreds of protesters arrested as demonstrations sweep across France over the cost of living crisis.
"It's the Revolution − we're taking the Bastille!" shouted protesters as they stormed the mayor’s offices in Marseille, according to Le Monde , drawing comparison to the French Revolution of 1789.
In La Rochelle, marchers held placards reading “revolution or death”, while in Montpellier signs read: “the people will win”.
Thousands of people spilled onto the streets early this morning to protest falling education standards and the cost of living in France.
Large groups gathered in Paris and Marseille ahead of the official marches and more than 150 arrests were made before midday.
Just a couple of hours later, huge demonstrations erupted across the whole country, with tens of thousands of people taking part.
Police have been out in full force, firing tear gas, using stun grenades, water cannons, and chasing protesters with batons.
French president Emmanuel Macron appealed for “calm” and called on demonstrators to show “respect for people and property”.
According to the Yellow Vests, one of the organisations leading today's protests, there were 1,756 mobilisations taking place on Saturday, including 811 demonstrations.
Masked protesters stormed Marseille's town hall after ramming the doors with security barriers in the morning, and were followed by attacks on town halls in Grenoble and Lille.

articles.title_orig: NYC Subway Shooting in Midtown Leaves Man Dead
articles.title_zh: NYC Subway Shooting in Midtown Leaves Man Dead
articles.content_orig:
A man died Saturday after being shot during a dispute at a subway station in Manhattan’s Theater District, according to police.
Officers responded to reports of gunfire at the 53rd Street and Seventh Avenue subway station around 12:21 p.m., police said. The victim was taken to a nearby hospital, where he was pronounced dead at 1:06 p.m.
The station serves Midtown Manhattan, an area crowded with tourists and theatergoers.
Authorities did not name the victim, pending notification of his family, and said he was “possibly” in his 30s.
Police are searching for a man in connection with the shooting. In a statement, NYPD said the man approached the victim on the northbound E train platform, shot him once in the chest and fled on foot.
At a news conference, police said a dispute between two men moved from the platform onto a train and back onto the platform. Investigators were still determining where the shots were fired, police said at the briefing.
Police said the shooting was not a random act.
The perpetrator “should face maximum consequences from the justice system,” MTA Chief Security Officer Michael Kemper said.
“It is fortunate nobody outside the fight was hurt,” he added.
Yellow police tape blocked the entrance to the Seventh Avenue subway station Saturday afternoon.
I’m a reporter on NBC News’ breaking news team, covering crime, extreme weather, pop culture and more. I recently covered Hurricane Milton, which devastated the Tampa, Florida, metropolitan area, and the student-led protests at Columbia University.
Meriam Bouarrouj is an NBC News assignment editor.

articles.title_orig: Brno 2027 unveils official emblems and branding
articles.title_zh: Brno 2027 unveils official emblems and branding
articles.content_orig:
Inspired by one of the Czech city’s most famous legends, the visual identity brings together the 20th World Climbing Championship and the 10th World Climbing Para Championship
With 300 days to go until the start of the competition, Brno 2027 has unveiled its official emblems and visual identity, setting the stage for a landmark celebration of Climbing and Para Climbing. Taking place from 13 to 21 August 2027, the event will unite the two sports’ flagship championships for nine days of world-class competition, with athletes also competing for qualification opportunities for the Olympic and Paralympic Games LA28.
Designed by Matta, the London-based creative agency behind the World Climbing brand unveiled at the end of 2025, the Brno 2027 identity draws inspiration from the host city’s cultural heritage, bringing local history and contemporary design together in a distinctive visual language.
At the centre of the event emblem is a shape inspired by the Brno Dragon, one of the most recognisable symbols of the Moravian capital. Despite its mythical name, the city’s famous dragon is actually a preserved Nile crocodile, approximately five metres long, which hangs from the ceiling of a passage in Brno’s Old Town Hall.
The crocodile is closely associated with one of the city’s best-known legends. According to local folklore, a fearsome dragon once terrorised Brno’s inhabitants and their livestock. The creature was eventually defeated when a visiting butcher devised a cunning plan: he filled an animal hide with caustic lime, stitched it closed and offered it to the beast as food. After swallowing the deceptive meal, the dragon was vanquished.
Unlike many similar European legends, Brno’s story has a physical centrepiece. Although the crocodile’s true origins are uncertain, it is believed to have been presented to the city as a gift from a visiting dignitary. Today, the preserved animal remains one of Brno’s most distinctive emblems, inspiring local sports teams, souvenirs and popular folklore. Visitors can see it throughout the year at the Old Town Hall.
By reinterpreting this unusual symbol, the Brno 2027 emblem establishes a direct connection between the championship and its host city, giving the event a visual identity rooted in local history while looking towards the future of the sport.
The event branding features two versions of the emblem: one for the World Climbing Championship and one for the World Climbing Para Championship. Both share the same design, with colour variations distinguishing the two competitions while maintaining a unified identity.
The accompanying Brno 27 wordmark takes further inspiration from Eastern European folk alphabets. Its bold, almost carved letterforms lend the branding a strong, distinctive character, reflecting the region’s cultural heritage through a contemporary design approach.
The colour palette features three colours inspired by Brno’s symbols and the Czech national flag. Red and white reference the city’s traditional colours, while blue completes the palette with a nod to the national flag of Czechia.
Together, the emblem, wordmark and colour system create a cohesive identity for the two championships, balancing the distinct character of each competition with their shared place within the World Climbing calendar.
Brno 2027 will bring together the 20th edition of the World Climbing Championship and the 10th edition of the World Climbing Para Championship, marking a significant milestone for both sports.
Beyond determining the next generation of world champions, the event will also serve as a qualification event for the Olympic and Paralympic Games LA28, adding further significance to nine days of competition in Czechia.
With the official branding now revealed, the countdown to Brno 2027 continues.

articles.title_zh: China’s Answer to Micron Just Made Nearly $20 Billion
articles.content_orig:

CXMT swung from a 5-billion-yuan loss to nearly $20 billion profit in nine months, giving China's state-backed chipmaker cash to threaten Micron's memory boom.
SanDisk dropped nearly 7% on the same day Micron fell 5.6%, reflecting its greater NAND exposure versus AI-driven DRAM that is lifting memory profits.
Micron's Q4 alone earned $37.7 billion, which exceeded CXMT's nine-month total, and its finance chief expects margins above any prior cycle peak.

China's largest memory chipmaker, ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT), told the Shanghai Stock Exchange on October 16, 2026, that it earned between $19.6 billion and $19.8 billion in net profit from January through September 2026. That works out to 131 billion to 132.5 billion yuan. The figures are preliminary and unaudited, so they are the company's estimates until audited results confirm them.
In the same period of 2025, CXMT lost 5.3 billion yuan. Micron Technology ( NASDAQ:MU ) fell 5.63% to $878.84 that day. The whole chip sector sold off, so CXMT's filing cannot be blamed for the drop on its own.
This creates a problem for Micron holders. CXMT's profit shows the shortage is lifting every memory maker, but it also gives a state-backed rival the cash to build the new supply that usually ends memory booms.
Revenue came in between 265 billion and 270 billion yuan, compared with 32.1 billion yuan a year earlier. That is more than an eightfold increase. CXMT gave three reasons: AI demand has squeezed the DRAM market (the main working memory in computers and servers) since the second half of 2025, the company added capacity, and it got more chips out of each silicon wafer.

Chairman Zhu Yiming proposed a buyback of 1 billion to 2 billion yuan over 12 months. So far, that is only a proposal, and no shares have been bought under it.
CXMT listed in Shanghai in July and jumped 466% on its first day. On October 16, shares rose 3.28% to 45.02 yuan, valuing the company at about 3.06 trillion yuan. You cannot buy CXMT on a US exchange, which makes Micron the US-listed stock most tied to this story.
Micron earned $37.701 billion in its fiscal fourth quarter alone. That single quarter is more than CXMT's nine-month total, and it came on full-year revenue of $133.19 billion.
US export controls limit China's access to the most advanced chipmaking tools. Those tools matter most for high-bandwidth memory (HBM), the stacked chips used in AI servers. Micron says it has completed deals for the "vast majority" of its calendar 2027 HBM supply. Its September 30, 2026 earnings call included no specific comment on Chinese competitors.
Memory booms tend to follow the same path. Shortages push prices up, the profits pay for new factories, and the new supply eventually pulls prices back down. CXMT now has the cash for that second step.
Micron's management argues the turn is still a long way off: "We do not have line of sight to when supply and demand will return to balance." Keep in mind that a seller has every reason to say supply is tight. Still, Micron backs the claim with more than 75% of its 2027 output already committed.
Peers fell more than Micron on October 16. SK Hynix dropped 6.58%, and SanDisk ( NASDAQ:SNDK ) lost 6.85%. The selloff left Micron's market value at $994.34 billion, just under $1 trillion.
Micron's share price has pulled back from its peak. The stock sits about 30% below its high, while the company guided fiscal first-quarter revenue to $61.5 billion ± $1.5 billion.
Micron's long-term supply contracts with customers also set minimum prices for its chips. Its finance chief said, "Even at floor prices, we expect margins meaningfully above any prior cycle peak margins."
Since CXMT trades only in Shanghai, Micron is still the US-listed company most exposed to this theme. SanDisk is more exposed to NAND storage, and it fell harder that day.
Two developments would weaken this outlook. The first is Micron's next earnings report coming in below the bottom of that guidance range. The second is CXMT announcing a large capacity expansion alongside its audited full-year results.

articles.title_orig: Davidovich Fokina upsets future No. 1 Zverev to reach the Shanghai Masters final against Jodar
articles.title_zh: Davidovich Fokina upsets future No. 1 Zverev to reach the Shanghai Masters final against Jodar
articles.content_orig:
SHANGHAI (AP) — Alejandro Davidovich Fokina upset future No. 1 Alexander Zverev 5-7, 6-4, 6-3 to reach the Shanghai Masters final on Saturday.
The 25th-seeded Spaniard, who won the ATP 250 Chengdu Open in China last month, reached the second Masters final of his career after losing on clay at Monte Carlo in 2022.
He will try for his third title of the year — and of his career — against 20-year-old Spaniard Rafael Jodar, who also secured a big win by toppling 2019 champion Daniil Medvedev 6-3, 6-4 to reach his first Masters final.
Medvedev saved three match points serving at 5-3 down and then held serve. But Jodar sealed the victory on his own serve, clipping a forehand winner down the line after Medvedev's tame smash at the net sat up nicely for him.
The No. 12-seeded Jodar is looking for his second career title after winning on clay at the Grand Prix Hassan II in Marrakech, Morocco in April.
Earlier Saturday, the top-seeded Zverev, who recently clinched the year-end No. 1 ranking , served out the first set with an ace.
But the imposing German soon found himself under pressure, saving two break points in the fourth game of the second set.
Davidovich Fokina broke Zverev with a brilliant two-handed backhand down the line to level the match, and an ace put him 4-1 up in the deciding set.
“Today I was flat. Even in the first set, even though I won the set,” Zverev said. "I was not reacting so well. I was returning quite badly.”
At 15-40 down on serve in the eighth game, Zverev saved two match points. But Davidovich Fokina held his nerve and clinched victory on his third match point when Zverev could not return his sliced serve on forehand.
“I feel like I've actually, in a way, maybe overachieved this week because of how much tennis I played," Zverev added. “I carried fatigue into the tournament, and I'm okay to lose to a player like this today.”
Zverev is scheduled to play the ATP 500 in Vienna, which begins Oct. 26 and could see him face seven-time Grand Slam champion Carlos Alcaraz.

articles.title_orig: China’s EV Transition Is Four Different Transitions
articles.title_zh: China’s EV Transition Is Four Different Transitions
articles.content_orig:
China has reached a stage of vehicle electrification that is easy to miss if the only number being watched is national EV market share. New urban buses are now essentially all electric, and in many cities the procurement question is no longer whether to replace a diesel bus with a battery bus. It is which new electric bus should replace the electric bus bought during China’s first major electrification wave.
That is a more important milestone than another record year of EV sales because it shows a transport segment completing its first adoption cycle and entering routine replacement. The International Energy Agency estimates that almost 70% of China’s more than 680,000 electric buses were already deployed before 2020, so a significant part of the current market consists of older electric fleets being renewed rather than diesel fleets being converted for the first time.
China’s 2025 equipment-renewal programme explicitly supported replacement of new-energy city buses and even complete traction-battery replacement, with the programme continuing into 2026. Policy is still involved, but its job has changed. It is supporting renewal inside a market where electric propulsion has already become the normal technology.
That replacement cycle is the starting point of my TFIE Strategy Briefing analysis of China’s electric transport markets . Looking across buses, cars, heavy trucks and coaches shows why “China’s EV adoption rate” is increasingly the wrong denominator.
Passenger cars are at a different point. Electric cars accounted for just over half of Chinese new-car sales in 2025, and buyers had nearly 700 electric models available by the end of the year. The IEA estimates that nearly 70% of battery-electric cars sold in China were cheaper than comparable conventional cars even before incentives, which means electric propulsion is no longer a specialist alternative for Chinese car buyers. It is one of the normal choices across much of the market.
Heavy trucks are behind cars in absolute market share but are moving much faster. Electric heavy trucks reached about 29% of Chinese sales in 2025, roughly twice their 2024 share. Their strongest markets are not random: ports, mines, steel plants and industrial logistics operations give trucks relatively predictable routes, high utilization and places where charging or battery swapping can be organized around the work.
That is what makes commercial vehicles particularly interesting. A private car may spend most of its life parked, so fuel savings accumulate relatively slowly. A hard-working truck can cover enough kilometres that lower energy and maintenance costs affect the business case much faster, especially when infrastructure can be concentrated at depots or along fixed corridors.
Intercity coaches show why even that logic cannot simply be extended to every transport category. Battery-electric coaches were only about 10% of Chinese coach sales in 2025, despite sales growing strongly from the previous year. At first glance that looks like a category lagging badly behind urban buses. The difference is not simply that coaches need bigger batteries. They compete with another electric technology that China scaled decades earlier than most countries: rail.
China ended 2025 with more than 50,000 kilometres of high-speed rail, while its railway system carried more than 4.5 billion passenger trips during the year. High-speed rail reaches almost every Chinese city with more than half a million urban residents, and it provides one- to two-hour journeys across many 500-kilometre city clusters and roughly four-hour trips across some 1,000-kilometre corridors.
A battery coach can replace a diesel coach on routes where road transport still makes sense, but it does not have to capture every long-distance passenger trip that might otherwise have gone by bus. Some of that mobility has already moved to an electrified mode with better performance on dense intercity corridors.
This is why national EV percentages can obscure more than they clarify. City buses, passenger cars, heavy trucks and coaches all have wheels and batteries, but their economics are very different. They operate for different numbers of hours, return to different places, carry different loads, use different infrastructure and face different alternatives.
A useful forecast starts with the work being done rather than with a single adoption curve. Fixed-route urban buses electrified early because batteries matched the duty cycle and public procurement could coordinate charging. Passenger cars followed as battery costs fell, model choice expanded and purchase prices became competitive. Heavy trucks are now accelerating where high utilization turns operating savings into a strong commercial incentive.
Coaches will electrify too, but their addressable market is shaped by what rail has already captured. That is not a weakness in China’s transport electrification story. It is evidence that the objective is mobility with less fossil fuel, not forcing every existing vehicle category to grow into an equally large electric market.
There is also a data caveat worth preserving. Chinese sources have historically used overlapping categories such as “new energy bus,” and successive IEA editions have revised classifications as better data became available. The precise shape of the early bus curve is less certain than the large pattern: urban buses moved first and are now saturated, cars are mainstream, heavy trucks are climbing quickly and coaches remain much less electrified.
For policymakers outside China, the implications are practical. A country with a low national EV share should not assume every transport segment will crawl upward at the same rate. Some categories can move very quickly once vehicles, operating economics and infrastructure align, while other categories may remain smaller because another mode does part of the job better.
That changes how public money should be spent. Rather than subsidizing every electric vehicle category equally, governments can identify the uses where electrification already fits the work, remove the infrastructure bottlenecks and allow those markets to move first. Buses, depot-based fleets, high-utilization trucks and other predictable commercial applications often provide clearer starting points than trying to make an entire transport sector move together.
China’s experience suggests that the mature endpoint will not be one smooth EV adoption curve. It will be several different transitions unfolding according to the work each vehicle performs and the transport systems around it.
The full TFIE Strategy Briefing compares the sales trajectories for Chinese urban buses, passenger cars, heavy trucks and coaches, including why high-speed rail changes the coach denominator and why replacement rather than first adoption is now driving much of the urban-bus market.

articles.title_orig: US debt interest costs hit $3 billion a day and jumped 8% in 2026—faster than spending, revenue, GDP
articles.title_zh: US debt interest costs hit $3 billion a day and jumped 8% in 2026—faster than spending, revenue, GDP
articles.content_orig:
The federal government’s fiscal year ended last month, and the final tally offered another stark warning about the trajectory of U.S. debt.
According to Treasury Department data released on Friday, the federal budget deficit widened to $1.99 trillion, 12% worse than the $1.78 trillion gap in fiscal 2025.
That came as revenue increased 3% to $5.4 trillion, lagging behind the 6% bump in spending to $7.4 trillion. Social Security and Medicare were the biggest line items, but in third place was interest payments on the national debt, topping defense spending and Medicaid.
Gross interest costs for fiscal 2026 came in at $1.36 trillion, Treasury data show, with an average interest rate of 3.53%. That’s more than double the rate in 2021, just before the Federal Reserve embarked on an aggressive tightening cycle to rein in inflation.
Net interest payments rose 8% to $1.05 trillion, outpacing increases in total spending, revenue and GDP. In fact, it exceeds real GDP growth of about 2% as well as nominal GDP growth of about 6%.
Fiscal 2026’s net interest costs translate to about $2.9 billion a day, and the Peter G. Peterson Foundation estimated they represent 3.2% of GDP, breaking the previous record set in 1991.
With gross U.S. debt at $40 trillion, publicly held debt at 100% of GDP, and borrowing costs up, interest payments are projected to be the fastest growing portion of the federal budget in the coming years.
At the same time, the debt burden is being increasingly exposed to market volatility that threatens to make interest costs even steeper.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has been issuing more short-term debt to finance the deficit and is retiring long-term obligations.
Now, about one-third of publicly held debt, or more than $10 trillion, is due to mature within the next 12 months, meaning the federal government must roll it over at today’s higher rates.
In February, the Congressional Budget Office projected annual debt interest expenses will reach $2.1 trillion by 2036. But then President Donald Trump launched the Iran war, which sent oil prices and bond yields soaring.
The 10-year Treasury yield is now above 5%, blowing past the CBO’s forecasts for 4.1% this year, 4.2% in 2027, 4.3% from 2028 to 2031, and 4.4% from 2032 to 2036.
If bond yields remain about 1 percentage point above the CBO’s estimates, interest costs will surge to $2.8 trillion, or 5.9% of GDP, by the end of the decade, according to the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget.
“Higher interest begets more debt, and greater debt begets higher rates and higher interest. Eventually, the whole thing could come crashing down,” CRFB President Maya MacGuineas said last month.
“That’s why Washington needs a fiscal intervention now, before it’s too late. The President, the Treasury Secretary, and Congressional leadership need to understand the severity of this issue. There are no easy fixes, and we can’t just wish this problem away.”
But so far, there’s no sign of much willingness to tackle spending or revenue. Trump has even called for a $5,000 “dividend” check to Americans if Republicans win the midterm elections and is already handing out “rebates” to millions of Medicare and Affordable Care Act enrollees.
Meanwhile, Bessent has argued that heating up the economy further can get the debt under control.
“With 3% growth, we grow our way out of this,” he said at Southern Methodist University last month. “We’ll get to the other side of this Iran conflict, and the underlying economy is very, very strong, and I think reaccelerating.”
But CBO Director Phillip Swagel said last week that faster economic growth is unlikely to keep U.S. debt in check . While stronger economic growth will help by bringing in more revenue for the federal government, it’s not that simple.
Federal spending also boosts growth, which lifts wages that in turn affect outlays on Social Security benefits, he pointed out. A robust economy also tends to send interest rates higher, which adds to debt interest costs.
Assuming interest rates of 4% to 5%, Swagel estimated that nominal GDP growth would have to reach 7%-8%, and real GDP growth would have to hit 5%-6% in order to stabilize the debt.
That’s more than double the latest real GDP pace of 2.2% in the second quarter. Meanwhile, even bullish Wall Street forecasts put full-year GDP growth at 2.5%.
“So growth will help, but it’s probably not plausible that growth alone will stabilize our fiscal trajectory,” he said. “So then we’re left with changes in revenues and changes in spending, and those are political choices.”
Jason Ma is the weekend editor at Fortune , where he covers markets, the economy, finance, and housing.

articles.title_orig: Taiwan Wants to Make A.I. Chip Smuggling to China a Crime
articles.title_zh: Taiwan Wants to Make A.I. Chip Smuggling to China a Crime
articles.content_orig:
Set Trending Topics as a preferred source on Google.
Anyone sneaking A.I. chips into China could soon face a criminal judge in Taiwan: The government in Taipei plans to tighten controls on exports of A.I. servers and advanced semiconductors to Chinese buyers. Economy Minister Kung Ming-hsin confirmed the plans in an interview with Bloomberg. Unauthorized shipments would then be prosecuted as a crime under the Foreign Trade Act. Until now, they have counted merely as an administrative violation.
So far, Taiwan has relied on a blacklist. Since mid-2025, Huawei and the chipmaker SMIC have been on the list of strategic high-tech goods, and Taiwanese companies need a permit to supply them. Other Chinese buyers could usually still be served, as long as the chips did not fall under the 2022 U.S. export rules. Going forward, A.I. servers and cutting-edge chips are to be added to the list of controlled goods across the board, covering all buyers in China, Startup Fortune reports , citing Bloomberg. Chung Chia-pin, a lawmaker from the governing Democratic Progressive Party, has already drafted a corresponding amendment to the Foreign Trade Act. The penalties and the start date have yet to be decided.
The move also reflects Taiwan’s close ties with the United States. In January, Taiwan and the U.S. struck a trade agreement that cut U.S. tariffs on most Taiwanese goods from 20 percent to 15 percent. In return, Taiwanese companies pledged $250 billion (about €223 billion) in investment in American semiconductors, energy and A.I., backed by a further $250 billion in credit guarantees. The stricter export rules are in line with Washington’s effort to curb China’s access to A.I. chips.
At the same time, Taiwan is cashing in on the A.I. boom. Semiconductor exports hit a record $87.2 billion (about €77.8 billion) in September, up 60.9 percent from a year earlier. The biggest beneficiary, TSMC, recently reported a record profit .
The problem is real. According to Bloomberg, Nvidia chips reach Chinese buyers through smuggling networks in Southeast Asia. In May, Taiwan arrested suspected A.I. chip smugglers for the first time, and in July, prosecutors went after Super Micro managers, albeit on forgery charges. Existing export law lacked a criminal tool aimed specifically at diverted chips.
China is a big market for American chipmakers. In its last full fiscal year before U.S. licensing requirements kicked in, Nvidia generated more than 13 percent of its revenue in China, about $17 billion (about €15.2 billion). The tightened rules for its H20 chip cost the company about $4.5 billion (about €4 billion) in charges. At AMD, China accounted for more than 24 percent of revenue in 2024.
Both sides are escalating the technology conflict. China’s commerce and science ministries have put forward their own draft that would restrict or ban exports of 40 technologies, including A.I., chips and solar technology, The Associated Press reports. Beijing has not yet responded to Taiwan’s plans. For already jittery markets, it is another signal after A.I. and chip stocks fell sharply in recent days.

articles.title_orig: Ilhan Omar’s Sister’s Phone Was Seized Before Search of Lawmaker’s Home
articles.title_zh: Ilhan Omar’s Sister’s Phone Was Seized Before Search of Lawmaker’s Home
articles.content_orig:
Minnesota lawmaker’s attorneys asked for return of seized items and the preservation of any recordings of search
Ilhan Omar ’s attorneys have asked the US Department of Justice to return property that federal agents removed days earlier from her home during a search.
The lawyers for the Minnesota Democrat contended that the seizure as “neither justified nor lawful”, according to a letter that the Associated Press reported on Friday.
The federal investigation into Omar was launched just weeks ahead of the 3 November midterms, in which Omar is on the ballot. Democrats accused Donald Trump, a Republican, of abusing his power as president to target a political opponent.
Omar’s attorneys wrote that there is “no legitimate basis for any suggestion that she has violated any law concerning her citizenship status”, according to the Wall Street Journal , which first reported on the lawyers’ letter.
“This vindictive, retributive, and politically motivated criminal investigation into one of the president’s chief congressional critics violates Representative Omar’s constitutional rights and threatens the separation of powers,” the congresswoman’s attorneys wrote.
The federal government has issued more than a dozen grand jury subpoenas, including of Omar’s relatives, and seized her phone in its investigation of the congresswoman.
A justice department spokesperson said the letter from Omar’s defense team was “riddled with false allegations and inaccuracies”, according to the AP.
“Our attorneys and law enforcement partners complied with all court orders and legal obligations, as they always do,” the spokesperson, Emily Covington, wrote in a text message on Friday evening.
The letter from Omar’s lawyers also accused the justice department of violating the agency’s longstanding policy aimed at avoiding potentially influencing an election. And they raised concerns about whether the investigators followed instructions from the magistrate judge who approved the search.
The attorneys demanded in the letter that the justice department preserve any audio and video taken during the search on Monday.
The justice department launched the investigation after years of Trump and conservative media figures promoting unsubstantiated rumors that Omar’s ex-husband is actually her brother – and that she married him so that he could obtain immigration status.
Omar, the most prominent Somali American in the US, has denied that allegation.
Citing sources “close to the investigation”, Fox News reported that the search on Monday was related to a criminal fraud investigation concerning Omar’s immigration paperwork. Omar’s father filled out that paperwork when she was a child.
“I’m ok,” Omar posted on X after the raid. “Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement.”
Omar also said the search was “just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation”.
The president has consistently launched racist attacks against Omar and other Somali Americans in Minnesota .
In December, he described them as “garbage” who “come from hell, and they complain, and do nothing but bitch”.
He said Omar “should be thrown the hell out of our country”.
After Monday’s search, Trump denied being involved in the investigation.
“I’ve always found her to be totally crooked, personally, but that has nothing to do with me,” Trump said.
The Associated Press contributed reporting

articles.title_orig: China proposes export controls on 23 AI technologies
articles.title_zh: China proposes export controls on 23 AI technologies
articles.content_orig:
China has proposed adding 23 artificial intelligence technologies to its list of technologies prohibited or restricted from export, while immediately requiring exporters to register covered transfers before they proceed.
The proposal is part of a broader revision covering 40 technologies across AI, biomedicine and solar power, according to a joint announcement issued on October 16 by China’s Ministry of Commerce and Ministry of Science and Technology. Public comments are open through November 15.
The proposed additions span large AI models, AI agents, computing clusters and information-processing technologies. The ministries said 14 of the 40 technologies would be prohibited from export and 26 would be restricted.
Among the proposed prohibited technologies are systems that autonomously generate or modify malicious code, as well as certain core large-model technologies trained with sensitive national data. Proposed restricted items include AI-assisted vulnerability discovery and technologies connected to advanced models, agents and computing infrastructure.
The Associated Press reported that the draft also covers some chip-design technologies, including those used for AI processing and memory chips. It said models with at least two trillion parameters, or with specified globally leading capabilities, could fall under the restricted category. The proposal does not name individual commercial models.
The other proposed additions comprise five biomedicine technologies, including areas related to cell and gene therapy, and 12 solar technologies covering polysilicon, wafers and cell manufacturing. The official announcement said the solar scope can also include key equipment that carries the relevant technology.
The catalogue revision remains a draft, but the authorities have introduced temporary pre-export registration from October 16 until the final revision takes effect. Covered exporters must submit information through the commerce ministry’s technology-trade platform.
The registration requirement applies to transfers of technology ownership, overseas licensing, changes that place a domestic technology owner or controller under a foreign entity, and other transactions specifically identified by the commerce ministry. It also covers transactions that have begun but are not yet complete.
The filing asks for information on the exporter, the recipient, the destination, the technology and its intended use, and the expected value of the export. Registration is not the same as final approval under the proposed catalogue, but it gives regulators visibility into transfers while the consultation is underway.
In an accompanying policy explanation , the commerce ministry said technologies already in the public domain through open-source releases or academic publications would not be covered. It also said most AI technologies would remain freely exportable.
For technologies that do fall into a restricted category, overseas deployment may count as a technology export. However, Chinese companies operating their own overseas cloud or computing centers, conducting chip fabrication abroad, undertaking joint research, or participating in international standards work may qualify for simplified or automatic licensing procedures.
The ministry drew a distinction between transferring controlled technology and providing access to services built on it. Overseas use through APIs, websites, apps and software-as-a-service offerings would generally not be treated as a large-model technology export when no restricted technology is transferred. Lightweight deployment on overseas devices would also generally remain outside that scope.
Reuters reported that this distinction could allow Chinese developers to continue serving international users while giving Beijing greater oversight of sensitive model transfers and overseas deployments.
The ministries said the proposed controls are intended to prevent misuse, protect national security and keep sensitive AI capabilities under human control. The commerce ministry said the move does not target any particular country, region or entity.
The final catalogue may change after the consultation. Companies involved in cross-border technology licensing, overseas model deployment or changes in control will need to assess both the temporary registration rule and the detailed technical thresholds in the draft annexes.

articles.title_orig: Official warns of China poll risk
articles.title_zh: Official warns of China poll risk
articles.content_orig:
Mainland Affairs Council (MAC) Deputy Minister Shen Yu-chung (沈有忠) yesterday warned of possible Chinese interference in next month’s local elections.
Shen made the remarks at the annual meeting of the Taipei-based Chinese Association of Political Science and an international conference titled “Rethinking Democracy: Continuity and Change in the Values and Practice of Modern Democracy.”
This year marks the 30th anniversary of Taiwan’s first direct presidential election. In 1996, despite missile threats from China, Taiwanese voters bravely went to the polls, marking a historic milestone in their ability to determine their own future through the ballot box, Shen said.
Over the past 30 years, Taiwan has held eight direct presidential elections and experienced three changes of ruling party, consolidating its democratic system while becoming a key partner in the global artificial intelligence and semiconductor supply chains, he said.
Shen stressed that the fundamental difference between Taiwan and China lies in their political systems: democracy versus authoritarianism.
Beijing has long sought to impose its “one country, two systems” framework on Taiwan and uses “united front” tactics to infiltrate the nation and spread political propaganda, with the goal of eliminating the Republic of China (ROC) and annexing Taiwan, he said.
However, Taiwan’s mainstream public opinion has firmly rejected “one country, two systems,” Shen said. Nearly 80 percent of the public supports maintaining the cross-strait “status quo” in which the ROC and the People’s Republic of China are not subordinate to each other, a reality that must be acknowledged in any discussion of cross-strait relations, he said.
The challenges facing democracies today extend beyond conventional military threats to include authoritarian powers such as China and Russia using “gray zone” tactics, information manipulation and infiltration to divide democratic societies and undermine public trust and unity, he said.
With local elections to be held this year, Beijing might continue to interfere in Taiwan’s democratic processes to influence voters’ independent judgement, he said.
In response, Taiwan must continue to bolster its democratic safeguards and societal resilience to ensure that its democratic system remains free from external interference and that people can exercise their democratic rights in a free and secure environment, Shen said.

articles.content_orig:

Expanding Next-Generation Network Capabilities and Accelerating the Innovative Convergence of Communication, Computing, and AI Laying a Solid Foundation for 6G Development in Hong Kong
HONG KONG, Oct. 17, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- China Mobile Hong Kong Company Limited ("China Mobile Hong Kong") announced that it has taken the lead in realising a U6GHz network, successfully completing network testing and validation at its Mong Kok flagship store and advancing the exploration of Upper 6GHz band applications in mobile networks. Implementing China Mobile Group's strategy of "strengthening the network foundation and full-stack innovation", China Mobile Hong Kong aims to enhance network capabilities through new frequency band applications, drive collaborative innovation between terminals and the wider industry, and lay a robust foundation for Hong Kong's future 6G development.
Strategic Early Deployment of New Spectrum to Build Momentum for a 6G Future U6GHz, or the Upper 6GHz band, can provide continuous wide bandwidth and is a crucial spectrum resource supporting 5G-A and future 6G evolution. On 29 November 2024, Hong Kong completed its 6/7GHz spectrum auction, becoming the first region globally to auction this frequency band for public mobile services. China Mobile Hong Kong successfully bid for 100MHz of continuous spectrum and has made appropriate forward-looking deployments, advancing network capability validation and terminal adaptation to accumulate experience for future 6G commercialisation.
Expanding Network Capacity to Enable Smoother Smart Applications The newly added U6GHz spectrum can be utilised synergistically with existing frequency bands. Through various combinations with current spectrums, it can achieve download speeds of 3Gbps. The increased availability of spectrum helps enhance data transmission capabilities, accommodating more simultaneous user connections, improving the internet experience in highly congested areas, and supporting high-definition video and large-capacity data transmission.
As artificial intelligence becomes increasingly integrated into production and daily life, the demand for data transmission from devices such as smart glasses and AI robots continues to rise. China Mobile Hong Kong will promote the synergistic development of U6GHz and intelligent computing services, enhance connectivity between terminals and intelligent computing platforms, and explore AI image analysis, immersive interactions, and industrial applications. This will allow smart services to better integrate into everyday life and corporate operations.
Aligning with Mainland China and Hong Kong Blueprints to Consolidate the Foundation of Digital-Intelligent Development China Mobile Hong Kong will actively align with the Nation's "15th Five-Year Plan" and Hong Kong's first Five-Year Plan. Focusing on "AI+", computing infrastructure, and new industrialisation, the company will enhance communication and smart services through network upgrades to assist Hong Kong in building an international innovation and technology centre. Concurrently, China Mobile Hong Kong will collaborate with industry partners to accelerate the research, development, and testing of U6GHz products. By expanding hotspot coverage according to demand, it aims to drive the maturity of the industrial ecosystem and accelerate Hong Kong's 6G development. Looking ahead, China Mobile Hong Kong will continue to leverage its strengths as a central state-owned enterprise, providing high-quality digital infrastructure to serve Hong Kong and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area, thereby fully contributing to the building of a cyber superpower and a digital China.

articles.title_orig: Trump signs order putting Russia sanctions on hold, drawing bipartisan anger
articles.title_zh: Trump signs order putting Russia sanctions on hold, drawing bipartisan anger
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump waived sweeping new sanctions against Russia passed by Congress, arguing in an executive order Friday that the move “is in the national interests of the United States.”
Trump had signed the legislation, named for the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C., just last month. The bill took aim at Russia’s largest buyers of oil and gas, allowing the president to impose tariffs on goods from those countries, which may include China and India.
Passed with bipartisan support , the bill was intended to target Russia’s revenue streams as the country continues to wage its war against Ukraine. Suspending the sanctions provides Russia a financial lifeline.
Trump’s decision to put a hold on the sanctions package comes after he announced a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin last week to release hundreds of thousands of tons of Russian diesel fuel onto the global market as fuel prices soar.
Trump has expressed frustration with Ukraine’s attacks on Russian oil and gas infrastructure and has blamed them for the increase in fuel costs while downplaying the impact of the Iran war on the oil market.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Saturday that lifting sanctions was “wrong” and “only helps the Russians.”
In a Telegram post, he decried what he called an “American sanctions blackout,” adding that a “weakening of pressure on the aggressor, effectively serving as a financial reward for Putin—only encourages him to continue his attacks.”
“It seems to me that this won’t stop Putin,” he later told journalists in WhatsApp messages. “On the contrary, he feels joy and happiness that there is such support.”
The decision to waive the Russia sanctions drew swift condemnation from critics in Congress.
Rep. Mike Lawler, R-N.Y., who’s running for re-election in a competitive district, said on Fox News Saturday that he does not support Trump’s decision, calling Putin “a vile dictator and thug.”
“I fully understand the need to get oil and diesel prices down, and we want to do that, but not at the expense of putting money in the pocket of Vladimir Putin so that he can continue to wage this illegal war in Ukraine,” Lawler said.
Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, who also faces a battle for re-election this November, said in his own Fox News interview that he does not agree with waiving the sanctions, though quickly shifted to acknowledge Trump’s support for Alaska energy.
Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., called the move a “craven, cowardly action” in a statement.
“These waivers have nothing to do with our national security, and everything to do with sucking up to Vladimir Putin,” Blumenthal said.
Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, said on Fox News Saturday that the decision “was a mistake,” adding that “the current path, unfortunately, just, it benefits Putin, and that’s not a good idea.”
“I think the president, understandably, is focused on diesel prices,” Cruz said. “That being said, people are hurting. People are feeling real pain. But there are other ways to address gas and diesel prices.”
“Beyond irresponsible,” Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., who is retiring at the end of his term, wrote on X. “What part of enforcing a law passed 86-11 by the Senate does the President and his advisors not understand?”
“If the President wants to actually bring down energy prices, he can do it by solving the Iran problem, not by doing a solid for Vladimir Putin,” he added.
Rep. Don Bacon, R-Neb., a staunch Ukraine ally who is also not seeking re-election next month, said “the president is prolonging the war, not ending it,” in a post on X .
“Lindsey would be appalled,” Sen. John Cornyn, R-TX, who lost a primary to a Trump-backed challenger earlier this year, wrote.
Zelenskyy thanked both Democrats and Republicans who supported the legislation, and praised the late Graham for his prolonged vocal support for Ukraine.
“He always supported us very strongly and pushed for as much assistance to Ukraine as possible. It’s difficult without him, I’ll say frankly,” Zelenskyy said. “And I am grateful to his friends who supported him.”
Trump’s move to pause the sanctions comes as the price of diesel fuel has shot up almost 70% since the war in Iran began in February and comes less than three weeks before the midterm elections, as cost of living remains a top issue for voters.
Sen. Darline Graham, R-S.C., who co-sponsored the bill named for her late brother, has touted its success as a key part of her campaign to win a full term in his Senate seat. Graham is a fierce Trump ally, as his endorsement was critical in her GOP primary win. Graham has yet to criticize the president for his Russian oil deal or the decision to halt the sanctions.
Congress passed the legislation with strong majorities in both the House and Senate, though many Democrats opposed the bill because it granted the president new tariff powers.
The legislation states that before the administration waives the new sanctions, it must submit an unclassified report to Congress explaining its basis. In his executive order, Trump said the White House has sent the report to Capitol Hill.
Kyla Guilfoil is a breaking news reporter on the politics team for NBC News Digital.
Brennan Leach is an associate producer for NBC News covering the Senate.
Freddie Clayton is a freelance journalist based in London.

articles.title_orig: Chwalinska downs Swiatek to set up Wuhan final with world number 170 Kartal
articles.title_zh: Chwalinska downs Swiatek to set up Wuhan final with world number 170 Kartal
articles.content_orig:
Polish 16th seed Maja Chwalinska overcame an injured Iga Swiatek to reach the first WTA 1000 final of her career, handing her childhood friend and compatriot a 7-5, 6-1 defeat at the Wuhan Open on Saturday.
Chwalinska will next face world number 170 Sonay Kartal, who became the lowest-ranked player to reach a WTA 1000 final with a gritty 7-6 (11/9), 7-6 (7-5) win over Jelena Ostapenko.
Swiatek, who needed to win the title in Wuhan to increase her slim chances of qualifying for the year-end WTA Finals, battled a left thigh injury during the match, which limited her movement against her crafty left-handed opponent.
Meanwhile, Chwalinska did well to manage the mental challenges of the occasion as she hit yet another new milestone in a breakthrough season that saw her make a surprise run to the French Open final, as a qualifier, back in June.
"Obviously Iga wasn't 100 percent today, so I wish her all the best, of course," said the 25-year-old Pole, who is contesting just her fourth WTA 1000 main draw.
"It's always tough to play against a fellow Polish player. She's a great champion, a living legend, she won everything. So it was a great honour for me to share the court with her today.
"I think I still don't really realise what's going on and the fact that I won against her is actually crazy for me."
The momentum swung back and forth in the opening frame before Swiatek attempted to serve for a one-set lead at 5-3.
The seventh seed could not close though, despite holding two set points, and soon found herself trailing Chwalinska 5-6.
Ahead of game 12, Swiatek took a medical timeout and was in pain and in tears while getting her left thigh attended to.
Chwalinska then warded off break points to scoop up the 80-minute first set.
In a bizarre opening game of the second set, a tearful Swiatek had an animated discussion with her strength and conditioning coach Maciej Ryszczuk on the sidelines, while facing two break points.
She was handed a time violation warning as a result and went on to drop a fifth consecutive game.
The six-time Grand Slam champion could not do much else to stop Chwalinska, who wrapped up the victory in two hours and eight minutes to set up a final showdown with Kartal.
Kartal, 24, is playing just her second tour event since returning from a six-month injury layoff, having suffered a spinal stress fracture that sidelined her from March to September.
In a close affair with 2017 French Open champion Ostapenko, Kartal showed tremendous composure and dug herself out of multiple holes to become the first British finalist in Wuhan Open history.
"Wow, that was probably one of the toughest matches I've ever played," said the Briton, who survived 50 winners coming off Ostapenko's racquet to reach the biggest final of her career.
"I knew exactly how she was going to play. At times she's unplayable and sometimes you just have to ride that wave.
"Mentally I think this is one of the best performances I've had in my career. I'm very proud of that one."
After dismissing three consecutive seeds in her previous rounds, including No.6 Elina Svitolina and No.9 Belinda Bencic, Kartal made the 35th-ranked Ostapenko her latest victim to reach her second career tour-level final, and first at the WTA 1000 level.

articles.title_orig: Albanian police fire rubber bullets as student protests rage
articles.title_zh: Albanian police fire rubber bullets as student protests rage
articles.content_orig:
Police in Albania have fired rubber bullets at antigovernment protesters in the capital, Tirana, as violent clashes intensify over demands for Prime Minister Edi Rama to resign.
The clashes continued on Saturday for a fifth consecutive day after high school and university students joined a broader movement against Rama, whose governing centre-left Socialist Party has held power since 2013.
The unrest has brought growing anger over education, unemployment and alleged corruption into a wider confrontation with the government.
Protesters threw stones, petrol bombs and fireworks at police near Rama’s office and elsewhere in central Tirana.
Some set cars and rubbish bins alight, creating burning barricades across streets.
Police responded with tear gas, water cannon and baton charges as demonstrators pushed against security lines.
The AFP news agency reported that officers used rubber bullets for the first time since the demonstrations began.
National police chief Skender Hita confirmed their use at a news conference on Saturday, saying they had been deployed “in a limited manner”.
The Ministry of Health and Social Welfare said nine protesters and four police officers received medical treatment on Saturday.
Hita said 167 people had been arrested over five days of unrest, while 132 officers had been injured.
Seven police officers were also suspended pending investigations into allegations that they had exceeded their authority.
Rama, who is serving his fourth term and has refused to resign, visited businesses damaged during the unrest on Saturday. He promised to listen to students and protect their right to demonstrate, while warning against further destruction.
He also accused his conservative political opponents of encouraging the violence.
The students have complained about expensive university fees, poor educational facilities and limited employment opportunities, alongside allegations of government corruption.
At the start of Saturday’s demonstration, protesters set fire to a suitcase and threw it into the Ministry of Education’s courtyard. AFP reported that the gesture symbolised their determination not to leave Albania in search of better opportunities.
“We are demanding our rights, our future and a better country,” journalism student Sinan Billa told AFP.
The student demonstrations have added to months of antigovernment rallies organised by the Flamingo movement, which began as a campaign against a luxury tourism development on Albania’s southern coast.
The project is linked to an investment company founded by Jared Kushner, the son-in-law of US President Donald Trump.
The movement has since widened its demands to include Rama’s resignation amid allegations of corruption against his government.
The unrest has also spread beyond Tirana. Local media reported that protesters in the coastal city of Durres damaged a post office and blocked roads with burning barricades, extending the confrontations beyond the capital.

articles.title_orig: Beyond depathologisation: Securing the right to health for trans communities
articles.title_zh: Beyond depathologisation: Securing the right to health for trans communities
articles.content_orig:
We all have the right to health. But when communities are pathologised and criminalised, the impact goes beyond basic access to healthcare. It leads to broader exclusion from day-to-day life, including access to safe housing, education and employment, which has a knock-on effect on overall mental and physical well-being.
Although the World Health Organisation depathologised trans identities 7 years ago , most trans people have yet to see the benefits of this groundbreaking decision.
While the WHO can issue guidance, it remains the responsibility of governments to adopt and implement them. Unfortunately, after decades of depathologisation activism, most countries are still lagging behind in the implementation of ICD-11 and its adoption into national processes and guidelines.
There are two critical intersecting issues that need to be addressed: access to legal gender recognition and access to healthcare .
The first is a key determinant in ensuring basic access to healthcare. Identity documents that match a person’s gender identity are a precondition for dignified care, having an impact not only on healthcare access but also on the quality of care, as mismatched documents often lead to discrimination and humiliation from health workers.
When people face discrimination, their general response is to avoid that situation in order to protect themselves. This is as true for trans people as it is for anyone else. In countries where trans people are criminalised, this becomes a barrier that prevents healthcare access altogether.
Therefore, when considering the issue of depathologisation, we also have to consider what other barriers might be impacting not only a person’s access to healthcare, but their right to health and well-being more broadly.
The OHCHR defines the right to health as including not only access to timely and appropriate health care, but also underlying determinants of health, including safe housing, food and water, a healthy environment, and access to health-related information.
When communities are criminalised or denied access to legal gender recognition , they end up facing discrimination not only in healthcare but in employment, education, housing, and sometimes even extending to their ability to move safely and freely in public.
There is another aspect to depathologisation that has far-reaching implications but which is much harder to measure, and that is the social stigma that comes with being viewed through a pathologised lens.
Trans communities are not unique in this respect, as many communities face discrimination on a similar basis, but what is unique to trans communities is the coordinated and deliberate attacks on our very existence at the hands of the anti-gender movement. Never have trans communities been more visible, and never have we been more targeted than we are now.
So what can we do about it?
The power and influence of the anti-gender movement is a critical factor here. We can only counter it by building collective power, uniting against hate, and organising within and across communities to push for justice, inclusion and equality.
In the vast majority of countries around the world, the third point seems like a pipe dream without the first two. We need to start considering the entire ecosystem that impacts the overall experience of a person, centring their humanity as a primary consideration, and reminding ourselves that, at the heart of the matter, is a person who is just trying to live their life to the fullest . Isn’t that what we all want?

articles.title_orig: Tesla Flying Car’s 4 Thrusters Meet Aerospace’s Bar [2026]
articles.title_zh: Tesla Flying Car’s 4 Thrusters Meet Aerospace’s Bar [2026]
articles.content_orig:
The flying car just got a little closer to reality.
Tesla’s long-awaited Roadster drove upside down along a curved ramp, launched into the air, rolled 180 degrees using bursts of compressed air and landed on its wheels during a livestreamed demonstration Thursday at SpaceX’s rocket test facility in McGregor, Texas, near Waco. Moments later, it used its thrusters to leap over a lineup of Tesla vehicles , including a Cybertruck and a Tesla Semi.
“Turns out the future does have flying cars,” CEO Elon Musk wrote on X afterward.
Getting one into customers’ garages is another story.
When Tesla first unveiled its second-generation Roadster in November 2017 , flying wasn’t part of the pitch. The company promised an electric supercar that could accelerate from zero to 60 mph in 1.9 seconds, seat four people and travel 620 miles on a single charge . Tesla began taking $50,000 reservations—or $250,000 for one of 1,000 limited Founders Series cars—and targeted a 2020 launch.
That date came and went. Musk has repeatedly treated the sports car as a lower priority than Tesla’s other projects , while also blaming supply chain shortages for earlier delays. On Tesla’s October 2024 earnings call, he thanked “the long-suffering deposit holders of the Tesla Roadster” and explained that the car was “not just the icing on the cake, it’s the cherry on the icing on the cake.”
Tesla now says production will begin in 2028—eight years later than originally promised.
The Roadster that took the stage Thursday is a radically redesigned car, built around the SpaceX thruster package Musk first floated in 2018 . It comes in three versions: Performance, a “road ready” two-seater with active aerodynamics and a fan-driven suction system; Thrust, a two-seater that adds rear-mounted cold-gas thrusters for sub-one-second acceleration to 60 mph; and Rocket, an invitation-only single-seater with 10 thrusters arranged around the car that can briefly take flight.
Tesla engineering vice president Lars Moravy said the thrusters run on about 600 liters of rechargeable compressed air. Tesla claims a top speed of more than 230 mph.
The redesign also comes with compromises. The original four-seat sports car now seats no more than two, and Tesla now promises a range of more than 300 miles —less than half the 620 miles it touted in 2017.
The airborne spectacle was a prototype demonstration, not a test of a production-ready vehicle. It showed only brief aerial maneuvers, not sustained flight, and Tesla hasn’t said how long or how far the Roadster can actually stay airborne.
Tesla states on its website that the Rocket version is “not approved for public road use.” It’s also unclear which regulator, if any, would oversee its flying features. The Federal Aviation Administration told CBS News and Politico that the vehicle doesn’t meet its definition of an aircraft, meaning the agency wouldn’t need to certify it as airworthy. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, which oversees vehicle safety, largely relies on automakers to certify that their cars meet federal standards. The Transportation Department said in a statement that NHTSA “will continue to monitor the situation.”
Musk, for his part, isn’t pitching the Roadster as a safe car. “This is not necessarily a safety-optimized car, OK?” he said during the reveal .
Securing a spot in line won’t come cheap. Tesla is asking for a $50,000 reservation payment for the Performance model and a whopping $250,000 for Thrust. The flying Rocket version is available by invitation only, with no publicly disclosed reservation fee. Tesla has yet to announce final prices for any of the three versions, and it hasn’t said what will happen to customers who put down deposits on the 2017 version.
Despite the hefty reservation payments, the Roadster is unlikely to become a major revenue source for Tesla. Unlike its mass-market vehicles, the niche sports car won’t sell in large volumes. At Tesla’s 2023 annual shareholder meeting , Musk said the Roadster was “definitely not gonna be a huge contributor to revenue.” Wall Street agrees: The Roadster “will not move the volume or revenue needle,” Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives wrote in a research note, according to CBS News .
Its value may lie elsewhere. TechCrunch described the Roadster as a “halo car” for Tesla—a vehicle meant to showcase the company’s technological ambitions rather than a volume seller. The reveal also came days before Tesla reports third-quarter results, which analysts say matter far more to investors.
The Roadster also occupies a curious place in Tesla’s future. As the company shifts its focus toward autonomous driving and humanoid robots, Musk has said the Roadster will eventually be the only manually driven car Tesla makes. Yet Thursday’s demonstration had no one behind the wheel—just a mannequin in a SpaceX spacesuit, a nod to the “Starman” dummy that rode Musk’s original Roadster into space in 2018 . Musk said the car operated autonomously for safety reasons.
For a company increasingly focused on taking humans out of the driver’s seat, the Roadster reminds us that driving can still be part of the attraction.

articles.title_orig: Ilhan Omar’s lawyers demand the return of property seized in house raid
articles.title_zh: Ilhan Omar’s lawyers demand the return of property seized in house raid
articles.content_orig:
Lawyers for Democratic United States Representative Ilhan Omar of Minnesota have demanded the return of property seized in a federal raid of her Washington, DC home, accusing the US Department of Justice of conducting a politically motivated investigation and failing to follow judicial instructions during the search.
“The political motivations behind this pre-election investigation and search are clear as day,” Omar’s lawyers wrote in a letter sent to federal prosecutors on Friday and obtained by The Associated Press news agency. “This search was neither justified nor lawful.”
In the letter, Omar’s lawyers, Amy Jeffress and Joshua Matz, challenged an investigation into her immigration history, saying there was “no legitimate basis for any suggestion that she has violated any law concerning her citizenship status”.
The letter accuses federal agents of threatening the separation of powers and failing to comply with a magistrate judge’s instructions for the search of Omar’s northeast Washington home on Monday.
Federal agents searched Omar’s home on Monday as part of an investigation into alleged immigration fraud. Authorities seized her phone and passport, and have issued more than a dozen grand jury subpoenas, including to some of her relatives, according to The Washington Post. Her lawyers also asked authorities to preserve audio and video recordings from the search.
Omar’s lawyers claim that investigators did not provide a copy of the warrant to them in advance, nor did they contact the House of Representatives’ Office of General Counsel, which disregarded the magistrate judge’s orders. The notice would have allowed Omar to seek legal counsel and potentially leverage legislation that could have challenged the warrant.
Her lawyers said the procedures outlined by the judge are intended to protect Omar’s constitutional rights as a sitting member of Congress, and safeguard against the seizure of materials related to her legislative work.
Her lawyers also argued that the investigation was politically motivated due to its proximity to the November midterm elections.
“Historically, the Department has refrained from this type of investigative activity so close to an election, so as to avoid even the appearance of politically motivated law enforcement actions,” they wrote.
The Justice Department rejected the accusations, describing the letter as “riddled with false allegations and inaccuracies”.
“Our attorneys and law enforcement partners complied with all court orders and legal obligations, as they always do,” Justice Department spokesperson Emily Covington said.
Omar became a naturalised US citizen in 2000 after fleeing Somalia with her family as a child, according to her House biography. She has repeatedly rejected allegations by conservative critics about her immigration status, which was also probed in 2019 during Trump’s first administration.
Omar’s lawyers have requested records relating to the 2019 inquiry into her immigration history. The former investigation found insufficient evidence of wrongdoing to warrant a full investigation, according to The Washington Post.
The scope of the current investigation remains unclear.
The search took place days after Trump attacked Omar at a rally in Tennessee, describing her home country as a place of “crime and squalor” and suggesting that Vice President JD Vance and others were investigating her. Hours after the search, Trump denied any involvement, telling reporters the matter was “really up to the DOJ”.
