articles.title_orig: Ukraine still unable to intercept Russian drones due to Starlink restrictions, Zelenskyy says
articles.title_zh: Ukraine still unable to intercept Russian drones due to Starlink restrictions, Zelenskyy says
articles.content_orig:
Ukraine is still unable to use its interceptor systems against Russian drones, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Saturday, because of speed restrictions imposed on Starshield, an upgraded military version of Elon Musk's Starlink, amid an ongoing row with President Trump.
"Unfortunately, we can't use Starlink or Starshield technology on our territory today to shoot down jet-powered Shaheds," Zelenskyy said in an online group chat with reporters at the EU Summit. "They fly, and we can stop them with aircraft and other air defense, but we don't use Starlink for that, unfortunately. God willing, this will be restored."
Zelenskyy said Kyiv was discussing the issue with U.S. officials, and he was told the restrictions were linked to technical issues. The Ukrainian president added, however, that Starlink appears to be operating at higher speeds on European Union territory.
"Yes, we are in dialogue at the level of the military, the Ministry of Defense and diplomats, in touch with everyone including SpaceX. Nobody there is answering our military or the Ministry of Defense now," Zelenskyy said. "At various levels they say these are technical problems."
"Here (in Ukraine) Starlink works up to a speed of 161 km/h, then shuts off," he continued. "In the EU it works at 180-plus and works constantly. Here it shuts off in the second minute after 161 km/h and stops working. We lose both drones and connectivity."
Mr. Trump told reporters on Friday he had not limited Ukraine's access to Starlink, adding he didn't believe Musk, SpaceX's CEO, was responsible either.
"Well, I don't know if it was anybody because it wasn't me, and I don't think it was Elon," Mr. Trump said while leaving the White House to travel for a rally in Georgia. "And from what I understand, it's the same as it's always been."
Musk said Wednesday he isn't responsible for deciding how Starshield is used, writing on X: "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS."
Starshield is essential to Ukraine's armed forces as it allows personnel to communicate and carry out strikes, including by maintaining contact with drones across long distances.
On Saturday, Zelenskyy said Russia carried out a large attack on Ukraine's energy sector, targeting more than 15 critical power generation and transmission facilities across the country. A day earlier, the president said the current restrictions on Starshield had left people vulnerable to Russian drones, which was "very painful and frustrating"
Ukrainian officials and soldiers told CBS News the country's military began experiencing sudden difficulties with Starshield equipment late Tuesday, including speed limits that made it more difficult to carry out missions with fast-moving drones. Sources in Ukraine's Ministry of Defense said SpaceX had unilaterally imposed the Starshield restrictions.
Mr. Trump has grown increasingly frustrated with Zelenskyy in recent days, blaming the war between Russia and Ukraine for high global energy prices. The Trump administration waived restrictions on buying Russian diesel last week in an effort to ease pressure, a move Zelenskyy argued could embolden Russian President Vladimir Putin.
In a social media post on Saturday, Zelenskyy called the move "unfortunate," adding the act, championed by late Sen. Lindsey Graham, "could have helped enormously." Later, he told journalists he believed the Trump administration will lift more sanctions on Russia.
"Unfortunately, the lifting of sanctions will continue. I believe the 'diesel deal' is just the first step," Zelenskyy told reporters.
"President Trump has been clear that he wants to see this brutal war come to an end. As talks continue, this Act provides the President with additional authorities to pursue a peaceful resolution," White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers told CBS News on Saturday in response to a question about lifting the sanctions. "Enforcing the sanctions provisions now would impede ongoing U.S. efforts to negotiate a durable and comprehensive peace agreement between Ukraine and Russia. The President retains the ability to exercise these authorities at any time if he determines that doing so would advance national interests."
Mr. Trump said Ukraine and Russia had agreed to stop striking each other's energy infrastructure — announcing an "energy ceasefire" over the weekend. Zelenskyy initially said Ukraine was willing to abide by such an agreement, but that Russia's strikes never ceased, and several days later he told the Financial Times his country would no longer hold off on striking Russian refineries because Russia was still attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
The Russian government never confirmed it had agreed to a ceasefire.
In a Newsmax interview late Thursday, Mr. Trump called Zelenskyy "not a good guy for us to deal with," argued Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries would be a "disgrace," urged both sides to make a deal and said the Ukrainian leader is harder to deal with than Putin.
"I'm not a big fan of Zelenskyy," Mr. Trump said.
On Wednesday, Musk had tweeted : "Time for Zelensky to go."

Kilauea's 55th eruptive episode
Kilauea has seen episodic eruptions since 2024. But after the previous episode ended Aug. 25, USGS scientists said changes in activity at the summit — including a series of earthquakes and a shallow magma intrusion beneath the Halemaʻumaʻu crater in late September and early October — made it impossible to predict exactly when the next episode would begin.
SCIENTISTS CAN NO LONGER PREDICT WHEN KILAUEA WILL ERUPT DUE TO RECENT VOLCANIC ACTIVITY
A magma intrusion occurs when magma moves into cracks beneath the Earth's surface, causing earthquakes and cracks in the ground.
Kilauea Message 2026-10-17 04:21:15 HST. The north vent fountain has grown to about 250 feet (80 m) high and is at least as wide. The fountain is feeding a broad sheet of lava into Halema'uma'u crater. Wind is from the northeast and tephra is within the closed area of HVNP.
USGS volcano observers said lava fountains have reached 250 feet in height.
"The fountain is feeding a broad sheet of lava into Halema'uma'u crater," the agency said on social media.
CENTURIES-OLD LAVA ROCK ARCH IN HAWAI'I VOLCANOES NATIONAL PARK COLLAPSES INTO OCEAN FOLLOWING HURRICANE NOLO
Volcanic gas that's released during eruptions can impact people downwind, particularly those with respiratory issues or other sensitive populations. Eruptions can also release Pele's hair, which are strands of volcanic glass, and can irritate skin, eyes and respiratory systems.
The Halema'uma'u Trail and parts of Byron Ledge Trail in the national park are temporarily closed due to increased seismic activity earlier this month.
Kilauea spews sheets of lava during 55th eruptive episode (USGS)
Image of Kilauea's 55th eruptive episode since Dec, 23, 2024. (USGS)
Another view of the new ground cracks in the north part of Kaluapele, Kīlauea summit caldera, cutting through the recent tephra deposits on the caldera floor. New cracks were up to about 6 inches (15 cm) wide. The active vents of the ongoing eruption are visible in the upper right portion of the photo. (USGS photo by M. Patrick.)
Some of the new cracks that formed on Kīlauea caldera floor between September 30-October 1 were steaming and warm (about 60 dg Celsius, or 140 dg Fahrenheit) when they were measured by this thermal camera on October 6. This area has been covered in warm, steaming cracks for decades, however, and there was no sign of magmatic gas associated with the recent intrusive activity. (USGS photo by M. Patrick)
Lava fountaining from Mount Kilauea Volcano. (Hawaii Volcanoes National Park's / Facebook)
54th eruption of Mount Kilauea Volcano. (Hawaii Volcanoes National Park's / Facebook)
Lava fountains from Kilauea volcano during 53rd eruptive episode. (Hawaii Volcanoes National Park)
Kilauea's 53rd eruptive episode on Aug. 12, 2026. (USGS)
Previously, the somewhat regular activity at Kiluea was being driven by magma accumulating in a shallow reservoir beneath the Halemaʻumaʻu crater. Each eruptive episode released some of that pressure under the crater, after which magma would refill the reservoir, leading to a relatively regular pattern.
The episodes were generally separated by pauses of two or more weeks.
4 CLASSIC TYPES OF VOLCANOES
Nighttime video of Kilauea's 47th eruption since Dec. 2024.
(USGS via Storyful / FOX Weather)
However, several swarms of shallow earthquakes and a magma intrusion shook Kilauea in September and earlier in October, opening new cracks in the caldera, which may have contributed to the longest pause between episodes.
Kilauea is considered one of the world's most active volcanoes.

A Bowdoin College student was removed from Thursday’s U.S. Senate debate after he stood and began yelling that data centers “are poisoning our waters.”
The moment came about 15 minutes into the fourth and final televised debate between U.S. Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, and Democrat Troy Jackson. It led to Collins quipping that it “was obviously one of Troy’s supporters,” to which Jackson replied, “Oh, shut up. I don’t even know that kid.” Thursday’s debate was the only one of the four to feature a live audience.
Henry Elgie, 19, was the protester whom security removed from the Gracie Theatre at Husson University in Bangor, according to a news release from the Sunrise Movement , a national progressive group focused on young people who are “fighting to stop the climate crisis and win a Green New Deal.”
“I’m so sorry to interrupt, but I’m a young person and I’m terrified. AI data centers are destroying our climate,” Elgie, who appeared to be wearing a press badge, shouted as security moved to take him out of the venue. “They are poisoning our waters. You are taking corporate PAC money to an absurd degree.”
Event organizers said the person was not on the pre-registered media list but presented a Bowdoin Orient press badge and was allowed in. In a statement Thursday night, the editor-in-chief of the Orient said the student paper did not send anyone to the debate and that the credential must have been fabricated.
A Sunrise Movement spokesperson said Friday that Elgie lives and is registered to vote in Brunswick, where Bowdoin is located.
The Sunrise Movement news release that came out late Thursday night made clear that Elgie was directing his words at Collins. It included a statement from Elgie that criticized Collins and her campaign for receiving donations from billionaires and executives of artificial intelligence platforms.
“Instead of investing in real climate solutions, Susan Collins continues to prioritize endless war and tax cuts for billionaires. My generation deserves a livable future,” Elgie said in a statement.
Collins campaign spokesperson Blake Kernen responded Friday by sharing a photo the campaign took of pro-Jackson and pro-Collins supporters who were outside of the Oct. 8 debate hosted by WMTW. A person in the photo was holding a fake check in the amount of $150,000 made out to 1820 PAC, a reference to the ProPublica story on pay-to-play allegations surrounding Collins.
The Collins campaign said the person holding the check last week was Elgie.
The Jackson campaign did not respond to a request for comment Friday morning.
Jackson supported the proposed moratorium on large data centers in Maine that Gov. Janet Mills, an outgoing Democrat, vetoed earlier this year . Mills cited concerns that the proposed pause on new centers until November 2027 would have killed a project in the mill town of Jay. (That project went on hold this summer, despite the veto.)
Collins aligned herself with Mills earlier this year, expressing support in August for projects at former mill sites and saying “there is usually hydropower right there, so there’s an energy source built in.” But Collins has also called for federal guardrails on data center development, including regulations on how much water and energy they use.
President Donald Trump has called for more data center development, despite public polling in Maine and nationally showing a majority of Americans from both parties oppose data centers getting built in their communities.

articles.title_orig: MN Senate candidates spar in the only debate before Election Day
articles.title_zh: MN Senate candidates spar in the only debate before Election Day
articles.content_orig:
It’s rare for a U.S. Senate race that doesn’t include an incumbent to only feature one debate, but that’s the case in the race to replace outgoing U.S. Senator Tina Smith.
Republican Michele Tafoya and Democrat Peggy Flanagan debated in the Minnesota Public Radio studio at noon Friday, sparring over everything from President Donald Trump to the war in Iran to fraud.
Tafoya initially supported the war, but now says it’s time to bring it to a close. “Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon,” she said, “but this has been going on now for seven months and Minnesotans and Americans writ large are hurting. The prices are too high. This war does need to end and it needs to end quickly. It also needs to end strategically. I would like to see the president lay out an exit strategy for the American people to listen to.”
Flanagan criticized Tafoya for her initial support for the war. “This war is costing us financially, but also in lives,” she said. “Twenty-one service men and women have lost their life, including a Minnesotan.  A mother. That’s unacceptable. We need to hold this president accountable.”
The two candidates also debated the impact of the Big Beautiful Bill, especially the lack of access to Medicaid and SNAP benefits for thousands of Minnesota families.
“This Big Beautiful Bill under Donald Trump has been absolutely terrible in Minnesota and Michele Tafoya has cheered it on,” Flanagan said.
Tafoya responded by criticizing Flanagan for doing nothing to prevent fraud during nearly eight years as lieutenant governor.
“And she’s talking about access?” Tafoya said, responding to Flanagan. “All of that money left the State of Minnesota, this historic fraud happened under her watch and suddenly she’s looking out for Medicaid and SNAP? Sell it to someone else Peggy.”
Recent polls show this race is too-close-to call. Our latest KSTP/SurveyUSA poll out this week shows Flanagan leading by three points, 45% to 42%, but within the margin of error of +/-4.2%. A Minnesota Star Tribune/KARE 11 poll showed Flanagan up by four points.

Last week, gamers still holding any hope that the GPU market would somehow stabilize had their hopes dashed. A while after Nvidia reportedly put the RTX 50 Super series on hold , rumors started flying that production of the already-rare RTX 5090 was stopping , likely to use precious silicon manufacturing capacity for more AI accelerators. Now, the company's senior VP Jeff Fisher reportedly said that card was not discontinued and would continue to be shipped. The statement comes after a myriad of websites, including Tom's Hardware , have asked the company for official comment, but to no avail.
The information comes from Taiwanese websites including 4Gamers and SJTV , which both are quoting a purported post-event interview where Fisher offered a brief explanation of the situation. According to the VP, supplies of the GPU are limited, but Nvidia is seemingly going all out to get the product to market (paraphrased from the Taiwanese reports).
"The supply chain (capacity) is indeed somewhat constrained, but NVIDIA is doing everything it can to get the product on the market. Although there are other variants of the RTX 5090 (chip), production has not been discontinued, and NVIDIA will continue to ship, which is very important," Fisher reportedly said to 4Gamers .
He also reportedly reiterated a common quote from Nvidia execs, stating that without GeForce, Nvidia wouldn't be where it is today, and likewise, the AI market wouldn't exist as it does today.
The claim that the card isn't gone after all merits some spot-checking, so we did a cursory browse of the common retailers. At Amazon , RTX 5090s are selling for about $8,500, but from third-party sellers. Best Buy has a grand amount of naught cards on offer, while Newegg lists 5090s for about $7,300, but from what are likely Chinese sellers, judging by the shipping time. The ever-famous U.S. tariffs would likely add quite a chunk of change to that price tag, too. Finally and perhaps most poignantly, the card remains absent from Nvidia's own marketplace and Micro Center as of this writing.
Some would say that these statements are nothing but a means to keep the company in gamers' minds, even though gaming-related revenue is now a vanishingly small piece of Nvidia's ever-larger money pie .
Jensen's firm isn't the only one seemingly keeping up appearances, as Intel has repeatedly stated that its long-awaited refresh of consumer GPUs isn't dead , and last year AMD said it still intends to deliver "the best mainstream gaming GPUs on the market." Yet there are no new GPU launches from any of the three, and their quarterly launch figures keep doubling down on AI.

articles.title_orig: CoreWeave Woes Risk Shutting Down AI Junk Market: Credit Weekly
articles.title_zh: CoreWeave Woes Risk Shutting Down AI Junk Market: Credit Weekly
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Neocloud stocks like CoreWeave ( CRWV ) and Nebius ( NBIS ) are poised to cap off a horrible week in their relatively short time in public markets.
CoreWeave and Nebius stocks are both down about 15% just in the past five days.
While concerns about CoreWeave's financial health are being blamed for the neocloud stock routs, the reality is that it's not just a CoreWeave issue. The overall financial health of the AI economic system build-out is being more closely scrutinized in a land of higher-for-longer interest rates.
Goldman Sachs explained the pressure quite well in a new note on Friday.
US dollar high-yield AI-related debt spreads widened by 25 basis points between Oct. 13 and 14, reaching a new high of 360 basis points over Treasurys. By contrast, non-AI-related debt spreads were only two basis points wider and remain below their March peak, Goldman Sachs pointed out (see charts below).
Within AI-related debt issuers, the widening has been concentrated in AI-related corporate bonds and data center project finance.
"While some softer AI-related sentiment can move datacenter bonds wider, especially if there is a reassessment around off-taker credit risk, we view AI-related corporate bonds, from either neoclouds or firms with significant frontier lab exposure, as being at the epicenter of the funding cost debate," Goldman Sachs strategist Amanda Lynam explained. "Further removed AI-adjacent Energy and Utilities have been more resilient, in our view partly reflecting more diversified revenue streams and a relatively defensive earnings profile. We think the widening reflects a reassessment of the economics of the AI buildout, particularly for lower-rated borrowers that are more exposed to higher-for-longer rates and potential energy-cost pressures."
Lynam sees "some near-term reversal" of the recent sell-off in US high-yield debt tied to AI. But she acknowledges that "dispersion across AI-related issuers is likely to remain high."

articles.title_orig: The Iran war has cost the average U.S. household the equivalent of almost $2,000, top economist says
articles.title_zh: The Iran war has cost the average U.S. household the equivalent of almost $2,000, top economist says
articles.content_orig:
More than seven months into the U.S. war with Iran, sharply higher fuel prices are making it more expensive to drive and fly and adding to the cost of some goods, prolonging the strain on American households as the midterm elections approach .
Motorists and airline passengers have borne the clearest consequences as the fighting disrupts Middle East oil shipments. Some companies have raised delivery charges or prices on selected products. Yet the higher cost of making and moving goods has not translated into across-the-board price increases at stores.
Shoppers may not be spared indefinitely, though. Many companies have absorbed at least part of their higher production and transportation costs. A September jump in wholesale prices suggests some businesses may eventually charge more if fuel prices stay elevated.
The chief economist at Moody’s Analytics, Mark Zandi, estimated this week that the war has cost the average U.S. household the equivalent of almost $2,000, including $1,100 in higher energy prices, $540 in higher interest rates and $360 in military costs. The energy portion is growing by $50 a week at current fuel prices, Zandi said.
Here’s a look at price changes since the war began and which goods and services could be most susceptible to increases in the months ahead:
BEFORE THE WAR: Regular gasoline averaged $2.98 a gallon nationwide and diesel $3.76 almost eight months ago, according to AAA. Gas peaked at $4.56 in May, below its 2022 record, while diesel reached a record $6.53 in September.
WHAT’S REACHED CONSUMERS: On Friday, the national average stood at $4.33 a gallon for gasoline, or 45% above its prewar level , and was up 68% for diesel at $6.33, AAA reported. Gas typically costs less in the fall, and this is the first October a gallon of regular gas has cost more than $4 on average, it said.
Expensive diesel is less apparent to most U.S. residents but contributes to overall inflation by raising the cost of moving goods.
WHAT COULD COME NEXT: Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remains dangerous and constrained, prolonging uncertainty over oil supplies and fuel prices. The Energy Information Administration said this month that it expected winter heating costs to be 21% higher for the roughly 3% of households that rely on heating oil, most of them in the Northeast, assuming the weather is mild.
BEFORE THE WAR: Jet fuel averaged $99 a barrel worldwide before the war, doubled to $209 in April and climbed back to nearly $195 in September after a spring decline, according to the International Air Transport Association.
WHAT’S REACHED CONSUMERS: Airlines have raised ticket prices and fees , trimmed schedules and shelved plans to add flights. Airfares cost about 22% more in September than they did a year earlier, the consumer price index showed. Average domestic airfares rose from $405 in late 2025 to $445 in the April through June period of this year, excluding optional fees, according to the U.S. Bureau of Transportation Statistics.
WHAT COULD COME NEXT: Fuel price volatility makes it harder for airlines to plan and could discourage them from lowering fares even when fuel prices start to fall, analysts said. United Airlines pulled some December flights and warned of further possible cuts in 2027. Fewer available seats could mean less pressure to hold ticket prices down.
Higher fares have covered substantial portions of higher fuel costs for domestic airlines but not enough to prevent a squeeze on their third-quarter profits, according to consensus estimates.
BEFORE THE WAR: The U.S. Department of Agriculture initially expected grocery prices to rise 1.7% this year, below the historical annual average. USDA now expects a still comparatively modest 2.4% increase.
WHAT HAS REACHED CONSUMERS: Individual food prices can be volatile , and it’s not clear how much of this year’s expected increase is due to the war and how much is due to other factors, including tariffs, unfavorable weather and higher labor costs.
Cornell University economics professor Chris Barrett said he was surprised grocery prices haven’t risen faster given higher costs for diesel, fertilizer and refrigeration. USDA revised its 2026 fertilizer cost estimates for major crops upward by 9% to 13% and fuel, lubricant and electricity estimates by 33% to 41%.
Barrett suspects retailers are absorbing some increases to avoid alienating fed-up customers after multiple years of food inflation . Grocery prices in September were about 22% higher than five years earlier.
WHAT COULD COME NEXT: Experts have warned that fresh produce and other frequently replenished perishables could respond quickly to higher transportation and refrigeration costs. Barrett sees “very little prospect” of a significant reduction in fuel prices that could ease the pressure on farmers and truckers.
A strengthening El Niño weather pattern could damage crops through drought, heat or flooding, the U.N. Food and Agriculture Organization warned. That could lift commodity prices, although ample inventories and good harvests elsewhere may limit the impact on groceries.
BEFORE THE WAR: Nearly all shoes sold in the U.S. are imported, and roughly 70% of the materials in a synthetic shoe are petrochemical-based, according to Footwear Distributors and Retailers of America. The industry trade group opposed Trump administration tariffs last year.
WHAT HAS REACHED CONSUMERS: Footwear prices were 3.4% higher in September compared to 12 months earlier, according to the consumer price index. Men’s shoes went up the most, by 4.5%.
WHAT COULD COME NEXT: While import costs are down from a year ago, the footwear trade group said oil prices, tariffs and geopolitical uncertainty are likely to keep retail shoe prices rising into 2027.
“Footwear companies are working hard to keep shoes affordable, but there is a limit to how much additional cost businesses can absorb before those pressures reach consumers,” FDRA President and CEO Matt Priest said.
BEFORE THE WAR: The cost of moving goods and delivering packages was already increasing and depended on more than fuel.
WHAT HAS REACHED CONSUMERS: It’s not clear. September producer-price data showed that transportation and warehousing of goods sold to businesses as inputs cost 10.2% more than a year earlier. Prices for truck and water freight services each rose 19.3%. The indexes measure what transportation providers charged but do not show how much of the increase appeared in retail prices.
Consumers have felt the higher costs most directly when sending packages. The U.S. Postal Service raised base prices 8% in April for Priority Mail Express, Priority Mail, Ground Advantage and Parcel Select, citing increased transportation costs. UPS, FedEx and DHL also impose fuel surcharges on many shipments.
WHAT COULD COME NEXT: Shipping costs could remain elevated during the holiday season even if oil prices ease. Third-party provider AFS Logistics and financial services company TD Cowen project record parcel costs this quarter and the highest truckload rates since early 2022.
“We expect fuel to drive elevated transportation costs for the foreseeable future,” AFS Logistics CEO Andy Dyer said.
Although UPS and FedEx surcharges could decline if diesel and jet fuel prices fall, changes to carrier surcharge formulas, holiday fees and tight trucking capacity could keep total shipping bills elevated, AFS said.

articles.title_orig: NASA’s Roman Space Telescope exceeds expectations by nearly 30%
articles.title_zh: NASA’s Roman Space Telescope exceeds expectations by nearly 30%
articles.content_orig:
NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is performing even better than scientists anticipated after engineers completed an extensive series of tests and precision adjustments. The work has brought the observatory's powerful instruments into exceptionally sharp focus, with its main camera system now delivering image quality nearly 30% better than predicted.
The achievement marks an important step toward the telescope's ambitious mission to investigate dark matter, dark energy, and other mysteries of the universe. Even the smallest improvements in optical precision could help Roman capture clearer images during its sweeping surveys of the cosmos.
"All of Roman's sweeping surveys will rely on the Wide Field Instrument," said Dave Hickey, a Wide Field Instrument systems engineer at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland. "Many of the mission's primary goals, like studying dark matter and dark energy, wouldn't be possible without it, so it's both exciting and a huge relief to see that it's working well!"
NASA Puts Roman's Powerful Camera System to the Test
Following the activation of the Wide Field Instrument in September, engineers began a comprehensive testing campaign to confirm that each component worked properly on its own and as part of the complete system.
Their first priority was examining the instrument's 18 detectors, each roughly the size of a sticky note, along with the electronics that operate them. The team then evaluated the element wheel, a rotating mechanism equipped with filters and other optical components. These allow selected wavelengths of light to reach the detectors and can separate incoming light into its individual colors.
Next came the instrument's internal calibration system. Engineers activated its light-emitting diodes, or LEDs, which function as adjustable light sources that can produce different colors and brightness levels under commands from Earth. By measuring how the detectors respond to these controlled signals, scientists can identify differences in sensitivity and make the corrections needed for accurate observations.
Engineers also tested the instrument's alignment mechanism and moved it from the deliberately unfocused position used during launch to the position expected to provide the sharpest images. They finished by checking the thermal control system, which maintains the temperatures required for the instrument's various components to function correctly.
"Calibrating an instrument is like tuning a piano or guitar before a concert," said Maxime Rizzo, a Wide Field Instrument systems engineer at NASA Goddard. "You adjust everything until it's just how you want it and then leave the settings alone so it performs consistently while you use it."
A Space Telescope Already Close to Perfect Alignment
While one group concentrated on preparing the Wide Field Instrument, another worked to refine the telescope's overall optical alignment.
The results were encouraging from the beginning. Roman's mirrors and other optical components were already positioned with remarkable accuracy, meaning engineers needed to make only minor corrections.
"The telescope's performance was excellent even before we began adjusting the alignment of all the mirrors and other optics, thanks to exceptional preparatory work done on the ground prior to launch," said Matthew Bolcar, Roman's optical systems lead at NASA Goddard. "All of the testing and modeling work done at Goddard and by contractors at L3Harris and BAE Space and Mission Systems left only small corrections for us to make to bring everything into near-perfect alignment."
Achieving that level of precision is especially challenging for a spacecraft. The forces experienced during launch can cause tiny shifts in sensitive equipment, and conditions in orbit differ significantly from those on Earth. Roman launched on August 30, carrying optical systems that had been meticulously tested before leaving the ground.
"Our ground testing couldn't exactly reproduce the environment Roman would experience in space, such as the absence of gravity," Bolcar said. "And there are also slight differences in temperature variations and moisture content. Despite those challenges, the recent assessments showed that our ground testing was excellent, with both instruments either matching or exceeding the performance we had predicted."
A Mirror Adjustment Smaller Than a Human Hair
Roman relies on an intricate arrangement of mirrors and optical components to collect light from distant cosmic objects and direct it toward its two scientific instruments. For the resulting images to remain sharp, the light must follow an extremely precise path.
Even a microscopic misalignment can affect how accurately the telescope brings light into focus.
Fortunately, Roman's optical system was already so well aligned that only incredibly small movements were necessary to improve its performance.
"We moved the secondary mirror by about one-sixteenth of the diameter of a human hair," said Alden Jurling, a senior optical engineer working on Roman at NASA Goddard. "This adjustment nudged the height of the secondary mirror above the primary. If we scale that height up to the height of the Empire State Building, the change in height is a little bit less than you would get by stacking a single U.S. penny on top of the tip of the tower."
Although nearly impossible to appreciate at a human scale, such a small adjustment can make an important difference when a telescope is designed to study objects across vast cosmic distances.
The team initially concentrated on Roman's Coronagraph Instrument, which had been producing images that were slightly out of focus. The problem was less severe than engineers had anticipated, making it relatively straightforward to correct.
The coronagraph now meets the team's demanding performance expectations. Engineers will continue refining its camera settings and determining the optimal configurations for its deformable mirrors, which can change shape to make extremely precise corrections to incoming light.
In the coming weeks, the team plans to test the coronagraph's ability to block unwanted light, an essential capability for observing faint objects near much brighter ones.
Once the coronagraph's focus had been optimized, engineers returned to the Wide Field Instrument for another round of adjustments.
Roman's Image Quality Exceeds Expectations by Nearly 30%
The final measurements revealed an especially impressive result. Roman's Wide Field Instrument achieved optical performance nearly 30% better than the team had predicted.
Before launch, engineers established an image quality requirement of approximately 90 nanometers RMS (Root Mean Square). This measurement describes the amount of optical error in the system, or how far the incoming light deviates from an ideal, perfectly focused wavefront.
To put that scale into perspective, 90 nanometers is roughly 1,000 times thinner than a human hair. At these tiny dimensions, even seemingly insignificant imperfections can influence the sharpness of astronomical images.
After the latest corrections, however, engineers measured an optical error of just 63 nanometers RMS, substantially better than the original requirement.
That improvement means Roman should be capable of producing even sharper images than its designers initially expected, strengthening its ability to carry out detailed observations across enormous regions of the sky.
"All of the images from Roman's cosmic surveys will be even sharper than we expected," Jurling said. "It's a great outcome from years of careful modeling, precision metrology, and testing."
With both scientific instruments meeting or surpassing their expected performance, Roman has cleared another important milestone in its preparation for routine observations. articles.title_orig: New drug reverses severe fatty liver disease by repairing the gut
articles.title_zh: New drug reverses severe fatty liver disease by repairing the gut
articles.content_orig:
An experimental drug developed at Michigan Medicine has reversed a serious form of fatty liver disease in animal studies by targeting an unexpected source of liver damage: the gut.
The compound, known as DT-109, works by reducing harmful gut bacteria, protecting the intestinal lining, and preventing inflammatory substances from reaching the liver. According to findings published in The Journal of Clinical Investigation , this approach successfully reversed metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) in animal models, offering a promising new strategy for treating a disease that remains difficult to manage.
MASH affects approximately 7% of the world's population. It is a severe form of fatty liver disease in which excess fat accumulates in the liver, causing inflammation and cellular damage. Over time, the condition can progress to cirrhosis, which involves extensive liver scarring, as well as liver cancer and liver failure. Although treatment options have improved in recent years, effective therapies remain limited.
"We see clear evidence that DT-109 protects the gut epithelial barrier, reducing the systemic influx of harmful microbial products that are thought to contribute to MASH development and progression," said Eugene Chen, M.D., Ph.D., senior author of the study and Frederick G. L. Huetwell Professor of Cardiovascular Medicine at the University of Michigan Medical School.
"This compound shows benefits to the gastrointestinal system and has great potential as a treatment for MASH."
How Harmful Gut Bacteria Can Trigger Liver Damage
Chen's research team had previously demonstrated that DT-109, a glycine-based tripeptide, could improve MASH in animal studies. A tripeptide is a small molecule made from three amino acids, which are the building blocks of proteins. What remained unclear was exactly how the compound produced its protective effects.
The latest research provides an explanation, revealing how changes in gut bacteria can set off a chain reaction that damages the liver and how DT-109 can interrupt that process.
Before examining the drug's effects, the scientists confirmed an important contributor to MASH: excessive growth of Clostridium perfringens , a bacterium that produces ammonia inside the intestines.
When ammonia levels rise, they can damage the gut's protective inner lining. Normally, this intestinal barrier helps prevent potentially harmful substances from escaping the digestive tract and entering the bloodstream.
As the barrier weakens, however, toxins and other products generated by gut microbes can travel to the liver. Once there, they can provoke inflammation and activate immune defenses in ways that worsen liver damage.
One response involves the excessive activation of CD8+ T cells, immune cells that normally help the body destroy infected or abnormal cells. When these cells become overactive, they can contribute to the inflammatory processes associated with MASH.
The findings help explain why a disease centered in the liver can be strongly influenced by events occurring elsewhere in the digestive system.
Experimental Drug Repairs the Gut and Protects the Liver
Through a series of experiments, researchers discovered that DT-109 disrupts this damaging cycle by improving the intestinal environment and reinforcing the gut's protective barrier.
In both mice and nonhuman primates, the compound reduced levels of Clostridium perfringens and lowered ammonia production in the intestines. These changes helped strengthen the intestinal lining, limiting the movement of harmful microbial substances into the body and reducing their potential to damage the liver.
The results were particularly encouraging in nonhuman primates, whose liver biology and gut microbial communities more closely resemble those of humans than those of mice. In these animals, DT-109 reduced liver inflammation and lessened the severity of MASH.
Together, the findings show how targeting harmful processes in the gut can produce beneficial effects in the liver, even though the drug acts primarily within the gastrointestinal system.
"DT-109 connects microbiota modulation with liver protection by restoring gut barrier integrity and limiting the systemic translocation of ammonia and other pro-inflammatory microbial products within the gut-liver axis," said Jifeng Zhang, Ph.D., co-author and research professor of cardiovascular medicine at U-M Medical School.
"We also found that DT-109 primarily acts in the gastrointestinal tract, but its reach stretches much further."
The gut-liver axis refers to the close biological relationship between the digestive tract and the liver. Substances absorbed from the intestines travel to the liver through the bloodstream, making liver health particularly sensitive to changes in gut bacteria and intestinal barrier function.
By targeting this connection, DT-109 may offer a way to address some of the processes driving liver inflammation rather than focusing exclusively on damage that has already occurred.
Potential Benefits Beyond Fatty Liver Disease
Researchers believe the compound's ability to protect the intestinal barrier could make it useful against other conditions involving inflammation and metabolic dysfunction.
Previous research has shown that DT-109 can reduce the formation of atherosclerotic plaques and prevent vascular calcification in nonhuman primates.
Atherosclerotic plaques are deposits of fat and other substances that accumulate inside artery walls, potentially restricting blood flow and increasing the risk of cardiovascular problems. Vascular calcification occurs when calcium builds up in blood vessel walls, making them less flexible and contributing to cardiovascular disease.
These findings suggest that DT-109 could eventually have applications in treating both liver and cardiovascular conditions, an important possibility because metabolic disorders often affect multiple organs.
The researchers are also interested in whether the compound could help people with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), a group of chronic conditions that includes Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis.
Because problems with the intestinal barrier are associated with several gastrointestinal disorders, a treatment that strengthens this barrier might have benefits beyond protecting the liver. However, additional research will be needed to determine whether DT-109 is effective against these conditions.
A Promising Treatment That Still Needs Human Trials
Despite the encouraging results, DT-109 remains an experimental treatment. Its ability to reverse MASH has been demonstrated in animal models, but researchers have not yet established whether it can safely and effectively produce similar benefits in humans.
The next phase of research will involve further evaluation of the compound, with the goal of advancing it toward clinical trials. Those studies will be essential for determining its safety, appropriate use, and potential effectiveness in patients.
"This study presents novel evidence about the pathogenesis of MASH and provides excitement about a therapeutic avenue to explore for a condition that remains difficult to treat," said Elliot Tapper, M.D., Academic Director of Hepatology at Michigan Medicine.
"What patients with MASH need is a safe and effective therapy capable of improving their liver and heart health - of course we are excited about these developments."
The discovery highlights an important shift in how scientists are approaching fatty liver disease. By addressing harmful gut bacteria and restoring the intestinal barrier, researchers may be able to protect the liver through a treatment that acts primarily outside the organ itself.
If future human studies confirm the benefits seen in animals, DT-109 could offer a new therapeutic option for patients with severe fatty liver disease while potentially addressing cardiovascular complications as well.

articles.title_orig: Verizon Will Charge You $10 A Month For iPhone Handoff
articles.title_zh: Verizon Will Charge You $10 A Month For iPhone Handoff
articles.content_orig:
Developers are now required to filter nonconsensual intimate imagery.
Verizon will offer Apple's new iPhone Handoff feature for iOS 27, but it will cost you $10 a month. The carrier says the feature is "coming soon" to its network in its announcement , where it also revealed that it was offering the iPhone Duo . If you'll recall, the feature launched on T-Mobile in the US, which charges $5 a month for it, and Deutsche Telekom in Germany. iPhone Handoff lets you use the same eSIM number on two devices, as long as they're both running iOS 27 and share the same Apple ID.
The phones can't use the same number at the same time, though — you'll have to choose which one is actively using the shared number at any given time. You will, however, be able to switch primary devices anytime you want. Your calls, messages and Find My automatically move to the iPhone you're currently using, and your iCloud backups are synced across devices.
To set up iPhone Handoff, go to Settings > Cellular > Set up Cellular or Add eSIM on your newer phone. Select iPhone > Continue > Transfer . To switch between your two iPhones, just unlock the device you want to start using. You don't have to do anything else: You'll just see a message that says "Switched to this iPhone" at the top of the screen of the iPhone. Apple advises making sure your iPhones have passcodes to remain in control of which one is actively using your number.

articles.title_orig: Cardinal Bernardin: An example for the Church and the world
articles.title_zh: Cardinal Bernardin: An example for the Church and the world
articles.content_orig:
We are publishing the full text of the Lecture delivered Friday evening, 16 October 2026, by Cardinal Blase Joseph Cupich, Archbishop of Chicago, as part of the initiatives carried out at Fiera di Primiero, in Trento, in memory of Cardinal Joseph Louis Bernardin thirty years after his death.
Cardinal Bernardin, born in the U.S. state of South Carolina to parents of Trentino origin who had immigrated to the USA, led the archdiocese of Chicago from 1982 until 1996, the year of his death.
The Italian towns of Rovereto and Trento are also taking part in the initiatives, which were promoted by the archdiocese of Trento. The three-day event concludes Saturday evening with the celebration of a Mass presided over by Cardinal Cupich in the cathedral of the Trentino capital.
I, who come from the city that Cardinal Bernardin called home, feel honoured to be here at Fiera di Primiero, where the Cardinal equally felt at home, thanks to your welcome and your esteem. Tonight, I would like to reflect briefly with you on how Joseph Bernardin took the best of what he learned from Trentino's rich culture and matured into a world-class figure whose impact on the Church and the world has not yet faded.
The historic speech he delivered at Fordham University in 1983, with which he introduced his famous âconsistent ethic of lifeâ approach to the examination of crucial issues of the contemporary world, as well as the leadership role he played in the drafting of the pastoral letter on peace written by the American bishops, offer insights into appreciating this impact.
There were three truly revolutionary beliefs that guided him. He was first of all convinced that it was necessary to follow up on the invitation of the Second Vatican Council to read the signs of the times. The Cardinal understood that the Church can only be credible if fully engaged in the world and attentive to what happens in peopleâs real lives, as well as to the forces that influence politics and public opinion. In many ways, he anticipated the famous phrase of the late Pope Francis: âReality is superior to the idea.â
His reading of the signs of our times led him to the conclusion that it was useless to address issues such as abortion, capital punishment, nuclear proliferation, use of military force, or anything else separately. He realized that this approach was motivated in large part by the fact that such issues were already divisive in themselves. But he was also convinced that an all-encompassing commitment to respect for life as a true principle connecting these issues would benefit them all. In his words: âThe purpose of proposing a consistent ethic of life is to argue that success on any one of the issues threatening life requires a concern for the broader attitude in society about respect for human life.â¦ The viability of the principle depends upon the consistency of its application.â
Second, the cardinal was convinced that the comprehensiveness of the Church's social doctrine made it distinctly capable of guiding the definition of such issues in the public arena. As a case in point, he asked how it was possible that only Catholic bishops strongly opposed both abortion and the nuclear war policies of the United States. It was the completeness of the doctrine, that is, its consistency, that distinguished the Church. Consequently, the social doctrine of the Church could not be confined to one of the political categories that characterize American public life. Yet this is precisely why the consistent ethic of life has attracted criticism. It affirms that the doctrine of the Church cannot be shaped according to our political divisions nor should it be diminished by minimizing the importance of its fundamental social teachings, even to approximate important political objectives. Along the same lines, Pope Leo recently observed that one cannot define oneself as a defender of Life if one opposes abortion but at the same time is in favour of the death penalty or does not oppose the inhuman treatment meted out to immigrants.
Finally, the Cardinal was convinced that the Church can count on a unique position to incentivize the promotion of the common good, through a redefinition of public policies. The way we cultivate faith, pastoral life, the ministries of health care and education: all demonstrate the completeness of the social doctrine of the Church. So much so that Cardinal Bernardin readily admitted that he chose a Catholic university to introduce his approach of coherent ethics of life, as he appreciated the particular role that Catholic universities have in shaping public debate.
The moral framework of a âconsistent ethic of lifeâ championed by the Cardinal is essential today, at a time when deep social divisions set people against one another in extreme ways. His sound counsel invites us to reflect on the risks of living in âbubblesââsurrounded by people like ourselves, yet fearful of engaging in genuine dialogue on a range of critical issues. Many of these are, in fact, matters of life and death: the healthcare crisis exposed during the pandemic; the scourge of racial injustice, which diminishes the dignity of immigrants; and the threat that climate changeâbecoming more evident with each passing yearâposes to all life on Earth.
The theological and moral legacy of Cardinal Joseph Bernardin remains one of the most influential currents of thought within the modern social doctrine of the American Church. As Archbishop of Chicago, Bernardin articulated a vision that wove various moral imperativesâfrom nuclear disarmament to the protection of the unbornâinto a cohesive whole. His legacy is fundamentally linked to two landmark moments: his leadership in drafting the pastoral letter on peace (âThe Challenge of Peace: Godâs Promise and Our Responseâ, 1983) and his lecture at Fordham University, where he introduced the âconsistent ethic of lifeâ.
Although he faced detractorsâeven among his fellow bishopsâhis insights were remarkably prescient, mirroring the holistic moral vision later developed by John Paul II in Evangelium vitae . It is no exaggeration to say that in Evangelium vitae , Pope John Paul II affirmed Bernardinâs broader synthesis, explicitly placing direct attacks on innocent human lifeâsuch as abortion or euthanasiaâon the same level as wider, structural threats to human life, including war, poverty, and ecological degradation. In doing so, he reinforced the principle that a true culture of life must take into account every threat to human dignity.
In more recent times, Bernardinâs words have gained new life and strength through the teachings of both Pope Francis and Pope Leo; both have championed a culture of encounter, mutual listening, and discernment, aimed at a shared path forward. We are the privileged heirs to the gentle and wise spirit that animated Cardinal Bernardin. As a successor to that good cardinal, I am truly delighted to be with you to celebrate his memory and his historical legacy. His words and his example continue to inspire us in our work for peace, the education and formation of young people, the promotion of understanding and collaboration among Christians and non-Christians alike, and, of course, the respect for life in all its precious forms.
I pray that the prophetic voice and the legacy of our beloved Cardinal Bernardinâwhich remain as relevant as everâwill continue to inspire us all toward an even deeper mutual solidarity, as members of the same family of God. We need this now more than ever.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine says Russia's claimed territorial advances are 'an illusion'
articles.title_zh: Ukraine says Russia's claimed territorial advances are 'an illusion'
articles.content_orig:
Ukraine's General Staff has refuted claims by Valery Gerasimov, Chief of the General Staff of the Russian Armed Forces, that Russian forces have captured 92 settlements since early September, including Kostiantynivka and Dobropillia, and advanced to within 5 kilometres of the outskirts of Zaporizhzhia.
Source: Andrii Kovaliov, spokesperson for the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, in a comment to Ukrainska Pravda
Quote: "Due to the lack of significant battlefield successes, the Russian military leadership continues to create an illusion of major victories for its own political leadership and domestic audience. The latest example is a briefing by Valery Gerasimov, Chief of the General Staff of the Russian Armed Forces, based on blatant lies, manipulation and exaggeration.
The General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine has evidence that refutes the Russian command's false claims about the situation along the contact line."
Details: Kovaliov recalled that in his briefing, Gerasimov claimed that since 1 September, Russian forces had captured more than 1,800 square kilometres of Ukrainian territory and 92 settlements.
The spokesperson for the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine said this was untrue. "In fact, thanks to active operations by Ukraine's Defence Forces, more territory has been liberated since the beginning of autumn than the enemy has managed to capture," he said.
Kovaliov also stressed that Gerasimov's claims about the capture of Dobropillia were equally false, adding that the city remains under Ukrainian control.
"This is not the first time the Russian leadership has presented wishful thinking as reality. On 1 September, Putin claimed that Sviatohirsk had been captured when, in fact, it was and remains under the control of Ukraine's defence forces," he recalled.
In addition, the General Staff described claims that Russian forces had captured Kostiantynivka and Oleksiievo-Druzhkivka and reached the outskirts of Kramatorsk as false.
"As of the morning of 17 October, Ukraine's defence forces still have positions in Kostiantynivka, where fighting is ongoing. Oleksiievo-Druzhkivka has also not been captured by the enemy, and claims that Russian forces have reached Kramatorsk do not reflect the actual situation on the battlefield," Kovaliov said.
The spokesperson for the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine said claims that Russian forces were advancing in the outskirts of Sloviansk and controlled more than 50% of Mykolaivka were also untrue.
"In fact, a small enemy group infiltrated the southern outskirts of Mykolaivka. Ukraine's defence forces are conducting strike-and-search operations to eliminate it," he clarified.
Kovaliov also commented on Gerasimov's claims about fighting for Orikhiv and the capture of Novopavlivka and Novoandriivka.
"In fact, as of 17 October, all three settlements remain under the control of the Armed Forces of Ukraine," he said.
According to the spokesperson for the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, the claim that Russian forces had advanced to within 5 kilometres of the southern outskirts of Zaporizhzhia is also false. The contact line has remained 22 kilometres from the regional capital for a considerable time.
"Another fabrication is the claim that Velykomykhailivka in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast has been captured. Russian forces have repeatedly claimed to have captured this settlement, attempting to present wishful thinking as reality. As of 17 October, Velykomykhailivka remains under Ukrainian control, and the contact line is 8 kilometres east of the settlement," Kovaliov said.

articles.title_orig: La Via Campesina takes to streets against World Bank-IMF in Bangkok, Thailand
articles.title_zh: La Via Campesina takes to streets against World Bank-IMF in Bangkok, Thailand
articles.content_orig:
Bagnolet, 17 October 2026 | Press release
For The Food Sovereignty for our Peoples, Against the World Bank and IMF policies! Our Future, Not the World Bank’s Choice!
Bangkok: On 16 October 2026, hundreds of La Via Campesina members, our member organisation in Thailand, the Assembly of the Poor (AOP), and allied organisations took to the streets of Bangkok to denounce the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) during their Annual Meetings in Thailand.
Their message was clear: peasants are fed up with the World Bank and IMF and their destructive policies. Chanting, “Down, down, World Bank! Down, down, IMF! Let’s Feed the People, not the Bank!” , protesters denounced decades of policies that have harmed communities, undermined livelihoods and threatened their future.
The AOP peasants and fisherfolk sang a powerful song that exposed the state violence and repression that many peasants face whenever they rise up to demand that their voices be heard. “We love one another so we are determined to destroy and annihilate. We love one another so we claim our father with such recklessness. We love one another so we burn our homes we burn our country. We love one another so we are led astray by wicked leaders.” The song’s bitter irony laid bare the contradiction between political leaders’ rhetoric of unity and love and the violence, destruction and suffering their actions bring upon the people.
“ Our struggles are connected. They are about the self-determination of peoples everywhere. The World Bank and the IMF have failed to support this right. We demand an end to imperialism and to economic policies that harm people rather than meeting their needs,” Hakech Mohamed from Morocco.
The placards told the story of how investment projects promoted by these Bretton Woods institutions affect people’s everyday lives. The peasants demanded: “Community Forests Are Life, Not Corporate Carbon Markets,” “Stop Blue Carbon Greenwashing,” “Stop Data Centres,” “The Future We Didn’t Choose! Our Future, Not the World Bank’s Choice,” “High-Spending Tourism Means Expanding Poverty,” and “Stop Land Grabs!”
For decades, large-scale infrastructure investments and economic reforms mainly in the low-income and lower-middle-income countries of the Africa, Asia and Latin America backed by the World Bank and IMF have contributed to the disruption of peasant livelihoods and the dispossession of communities.
Anuka from Sri Lanka, echoed similar calls to resist corporate takeover of our countries.
“ We are not here to negotiate. We demand our government to listen to us, the people. Mandates come from us, the people and not the World Bank. Cancel the debt! We don’t want to pay the debt!
“ We’ve come here to deliver our solidarity statement because people around the world are dying of hunger, and this hunger is linked to the debt crisis. Our governments are unable to take care of their people. At the same time, power is being taken away from food producers and transferred to multinational corporations that produce food, but that food doesn’t necessarily reach the people who need it .” Said Themba Chauke from South Africa
Peasants did not simply denounce the World Bank and IMF; they asserted their right to determine their own development, their future, and their relationship with their land and territories. Their demands included “Our Land, Our Voice, Our Future,” “Free Seeds, UNDROP Now,” “Peasant Agroecology Is the Solution,” and “Farmers’ Welfare: Restore Fair Crop Price Support.”
“Today is a day of resistance. For us, the Indigenous peoples and peasants, women and men from Latin America, we say no to debt and no to the Bank. The World Bank’s politics are politics of debt, poverty and the destruction of our peoples and territories. We have a proposal for life. We want to build a social contract in which peoples’ sovereignty and food sovereignty are prioritised,” said Maria Macz from Guatemala.
On this day, La Via Campesina marked the International Day of Action for Peoples’ Food Sovereignty and Against Transnational Corporations , denouncing the neoliberal policies of the World Bank and IMF and demanding an alternative grounded in food sovereignty and financial sovereignty.

articles.title_orig: A 26-year-old felt her concerns were being dismissed. Then she was diagnosed with breast cancer.
articles.title_zh: A 26-year-old felt her concerns were being dismissed. Then she was diagnosed with breast cancer.
articles.content_orig:
Andrea de Armas knew the ultrasound technician thought she was overreacting.
De Armas was 26. She had no known family history of breast cancer . But she had found a lump in her breast. Before beginning a rigorous program to train as a physician assistant, she wanted to get it checked out.
Being that young in a waiting room filled with older patients getting routine scans was already unsettling, she said. Then the technician seemed to dismiss her concerns.
"The tech had 'Why are you here?' vibes. Without her explicitly saying that, that's exactly what she told me. I felt belittled and just weird," De Armas recalled. "I was like, 'I have a mass, I feel something on my chest or breast.' And they were like, 'Oh, really?' ... It was just really uncomfortable the entire visit."
After the scan, a radiologist reviewed it and recommended that De Armas get a biopsy immediately. It was a sharp turn from the technician's skepticism, De Armas said, adding that she "had a lot of emotions and felt so conflicted" about the experience.
De Armas made an appointment at Baptist Health's Herbert Wertheim Cancer Institute, which did another scan and biopsy. Four days later, the day before her physician assistant program was set to begin, she learned the lump was malignant. She had breast cancer .
"Words can't describe it. It's just sensory. I was in a paused state, where I was just listening," De Armas said. "Then the words went through my head, and I felt like I was in go mode. Like, I need to do something about this, because tomorrow, I start PA school. So we need to do something about this."
About one in 10 new breast cancer diagnoses are in women under 45, according to the American Cancer Society's website , though only about one in 1,344 women are diagnosed in their 20s. Breast cancer incidence rates have also increased by about 1% per year, and there are slightly more new cases being diagnosed in women under 50 than women above 50, the ACS says.
Young women tend to be diagnosed with breast cancer at a later stage and tend to have "more aggressive" tumors or be diagnosed with rarer disease subtypes , said Dr. Mary Gemignani, the director of the Women's Early Onset Cancer Program and chief of the Division of Breast Surgery at NYU Langone.
Despite those statistics, some young women still face dismissal, Gemignani said.
"I've seen many women over the years who will give the story that they were told they were too young to have breast cancer," said Gemignani, who has been seeing patients for over 25 years, in a 2025 interview with CBS News. Gemignani was not involved in De Armas' care.
Further testing found De Armas had a genetic mutation associated with increased breast cancer risk. Learning that helped De Armas feel in control as she began treatment.
"It was a bit of relief, in the sense of understanding where this could have come from, and that there were things out of my control," De Armas said. "It's also pretty empowering for my family. People can get the screenings they need and get ahead."
De Armas was determined not to let the diagnosis disrupt her life. She had a lumpectomy in early June, a month after her diagnosis, during a break in her school schedule. To balance her program and chemotherapy, she went for treatment at 6:50 a.m., then spent the afternoon in class. She scheduled a bilateral mastectomy and reconstruction during winter break.
Gemignani said it's not unusual for young women to have "unique needs" when it comes to cancer treatment, since they may be juggling school, work or family obligations with less support or resources than older generations.
Dr. Cristina Lopez-Penalver, a surgical oncologist at Baptist Health's Herbert Wertheim Cancer Institute who treated De Armas, said the unusual treatment schedule allowed her to stay on track at school while maintaining her health.
"We worked together as a team," Lopez-Penalver said. "She was really not about ready to let this breast cancer get in her way."
De Armas graduated as a physician assistant in 2025. One month later, she was working in the field. In September, she celebrated her first anniversary at that job.
Now 30, De Armas says she is cancer-free. The days of surgery and chemotherapy are behind her. But because of the makeup of her cancer, she remains on hormone therapy. The medication put her into temporary menopause, which Gemignani said is another unique concern for young breast cancer patients . She also had to make fertility decisions earlier than she expected. She continues to see her oncologist for regular follow-ups.
"I'm really lucky. I feel like I'm doing OK," De Armas said. "It took me a little bit to kind of adjust. It wasn't immediate; it took time. It took understanding the kind of changes my body was going through. But I'm able to live a pretty normal life for a 30-year-old."
De Armas said she hopes sharing her story will inspire others to trust themselves and push for answers when something feels wrong. Being nervous about a scan or medical intervention is "a valid experience," she said, but someone should "never let the fear of the unknown freak you out."
"It's always in your hands, and you just need to just take the step together with community and people around you," De Armas said. "Just do what's in your best interest, always. We're all human beings. The things we're genetically predisposed to are out of our control. So to feel empowered, do the things that we know are in our control. It's a cliché that knowledge is power, but it is so true."
Edited by Lucia I Suarez Sang

articles.title_orig: CDC to send ‘disease detective’ to help tackle Pennsylvania measles outbreak
articles.title_zh: CDC to send ‘disease detective’ to help tackle Pennsylvania measles outbreak
articles.content_orig:
State has confirmed six measles-related deaths and county at center of outbreak lacks its own health department
The county at the center of Pennsylvania’s measles outbreak is at a clear disadvantage because, local officials say, it lacks its own health department and it will now get special assistance from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
As of Wednesday, Pennsylvania had confirmed 1,222 measles cases, up from 86 the week before. Six measles-associated deaths have also been confirmed by the state.
The CDC announced on Thursday it would send a scientist – specifically, a “disease detective” – from the agency’s epidemic intelligence service to help tackle Pennsylvania’s growing outbreak.
“CDC will continue working closely with Pennsylvania health officials to provide the expertise and support needed to respond to the outbreak and protect public health,” a CDC spokesperson told NBC News on Thursday.
The spokesperson also added that the CDC director, Dr Erica Schwartz, recommends the MMR vaccine “as the most effective way to prevent measles and protect against infection”.
The network also reported that in addition to the deployment of the “disease detective,” the CDC was releasing nearly $4m to aid the measles response efforts in Pennsylvania.
Lancaster county, the focus of the state’s outbreak with more than 415 confirmed cases as of 9 October, is the largest county in the state to not have its own health department. The plain community, or Amish, who have historically had lower rates of vaccination, make up about 8% of the county’s population.
The Guardian reported earlier this month that the state was bracing for a wave of measles cases, with some public health officials sharing concern that it was “only a matter of time” until the disease spread beyond the outbreak’s center.
The outbreak also comes amid concerns that public health in the US has been hit by growing vaccine skepticism, particularly because of the influence of the controversial health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr . Kennedy has also notably had a public dispute with the Pennsylvania governor, Josh Shapiro, who has lambasted the administration and Kennedy for spreading vaccine misinformation.
“I made very clear that his actions and the rhetoric that’s coming from this administration are having a negative impact on communities across America, particularly right here in Pennsylvania,” Shapiro said in August during a briefing to report two measles deaths in his state, their first in three decades.
He continued: “There’s real-life consequences to spreading misinformation. There’s real-life consequences to scaring people.”
Alice Yoder, who was elected to the Lancaster county board of commissioners in 2023 and previously worked as a critical care nurse, told the Guardian that county officials were “very concerned” about the outbreak and that, without its own health department, the county was at a clear disadvantage.
“It’s a lot for our state to handle from a communication standpoint,” Yoder said. “They’re perhaps doing the best that they can, knowing that Pennsylvania has 67 counties, with 60 being under the auspices of the centralized state system rather than having their own health departments.”
She added: “By having a local health department, particularly one of our size, I believe it would mean we would have local data, it would be in real time, and we would have that information quickly. And most importantly, we would have an established staff, which has established relationships with a variety of partners within our community, which means that once we find a sign of an outbreak we would be able to respond to it really quickly.”
Yoder, who is now advocating for the county to establish its own health department, added that because the county doesn’t have one, she and her colleagues find out about measles cases and deaths only through media announcements at the same time as the general public.
“I never thought I would see measles again in my lifetime, but once it occurred I thought that we probably should have been prepared for it,” she said.
An advantage for counties in Pennsylvania that do have their own health departments, such as Montgomery, is their ability to work with local community health initiatives, like coalitions aimed at promoting immunity.
Susan Wenrick, vice-chair of the Montgomery County Immunization Coalition, which is made up of members of county government, healthcare professionals and other community members, said one of the coalition’s main goals was to improve access to vaccines.
“The biggest challenges to vaccinating people in Montgomery county have been access and availability, but one positive thing that came out of the pandemic was the public-private partnerships that were created to bring vaccines to communities, along with addressing the uninsured and underinsured barrier,” Wenrick said.
She added: “These are challenging times due to the amount of misinformation that is available, along with the average person turning to Google or social media for their health information instead of consulting their healthcare professional. A big part of MCIC’s efforts is to provide trusted resources for all.”
As of Friday, the CDC reported 4,410 measles cases nationwide, marking an ​increase of 330 from its update last week. As noted by Reuters , ​the CDC “shifted to using mortality data from ​the National Center for Health Statistics for measles-related deaths, rather than ‌relying ⁠on state health departments, a change that has drawn scrutiny”.

articles.title_orig: Pope Leo XIV calls world hunger a ‘terrible offense’ against human dignity
articles.title_zh: Pope Leo XIV calls world hunger a ‘terrible offense’ against human dignity
articles.content_orig:
The pontiff, still hospitalized after surgery, sent a message for World Food Day on Friday.
Pope Leo XIV on Friday called world hunger a “terrible offense” against human dignity and emphasized that adequate food is a basic human right.
“It is a terrible offense against human dignity to prevent bread from reaching any person or to destroy the means by which it is produced,” the pontiff wrote in a message published for World Food Day.
Still recovering from surgery at Rome’s Gemelli Hospital, Leo addressed his message to Qu Dongyu, director general of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO). World Food Day, celebrated every year on Oct. 16 to highlight world hunger, also marks the organization’s founding in 1945.
In his message, Leo lamented the challenge of world hunger and questioned how some can speak of technological innovation while food shortages persist.
“Hunger cannot be considered a statistical anomaly, for it is caused mainly by a lack of political will and collective charity,” Leo said.
“Today, people speak of innovation with great confidence,” Leo said. “However, this term is often used only in reference to the development of devices and algorithms, or the optimization of performance merely for the sake of financial gain.”
According to FAO’s annual report for 2025, an estimated 645 million people worldwide experienced hunger, mainly distributed across Africa, Asia, Latin America, and the Caribbean. According to the same report, 35.5 million children were severely malnourished, and war remained the “primary driver of acute food insecurity and malnutrition.”
Leo also said that food shortages should never be “used as a weapon of war” and encouraged the United Nations to work toward a “new global food order” in which technology ensures food for all.
“Regular access to safe, adequate and sufficient food, in keeping with the dignity of every person, is a basic human right,” the pope wrote.
“A new global food order is essential — one in which technological innovation is unconditionally subordinated to respect for God-given human dignity and the universal common good.”
The pope’s remarks on world hunger follow his June visit to the headquarters of the World Food Programme in Rome, where he emphasized the need to focus on humanity to combat hunger worldwide.

articles.title_orig: Oregon father is the latest armed civilian to confront a gunman in a US mass shooting
articles.title_zh: Oregon father is the latest armed civilian to confront a gunman in a US mass shooting
articles.content_orig:
Authorities are investigating what led a 16-year-old shooter to force entry into his former elementary school in Bend, Oregon, and fire into a special needs classroom on Thursday, killing three children and a young teacher.
“Everyone wants to know why, including us,” Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said at a news conference Friday.
The shooter, identified by police as Griffin J. John II, had climbed over the Silver Rail Elementary School campus fence around 1 p.m. before firing at a witness in a pickup truck who verbally confronted him, according to Bend police.
The suspect then forced his way into the school by firing into the glass panes of an external set of double doors, police said. He fired multiple rounds into the special needs classroom that included students of mixed ages. A teacher attempted to disarm the shooter and a 36-year-old parent ultimately fatally shot John with a pistol.
The stream of gunfire left three children, ages 5, 8 and 11, and a 25-year-old teacher dead. Two others, a 7-year-old child and a 54-year-old teacher, sustained critical injuries.
Police are now investigating a potential motive in the shooting, including if there were any mental health concerns or warning signs, according to Krantz.
The shooter’s parents were interviewed on Thursday and were cooperative with investigators, a senior law enforcement official briefed on the investigation told CNN. Authorities also searched the shooter’s home Thursday, with investigators recovering computers and other electronic devices, according to the source.
Here’s what we know about the teenage shooter as the investigation into the tragedy plays out:
John used a Maverick 88 pump-action 12-gauge shotgun in the attack, Krantz said. The gun had been purchased by his mother, a senior law enforcement official briefed on the investigation told CNN earlier Friday.
Three types of ammunition were used by the gunman over the course of the shooting: 12-gauge birdshot, buckshot and slugs, according to Krantz. John had about 44 remaining rounds of ammunition, Krantz said.
In Oregon, a 16-year-old cannot legally purchase a shotgun but may legally possess one if it was transferred or provided by a parent and may lawfully temporarily possess it for hunting, target practice or shooting sports.
The shooter’s mother spoke to CNN off camera from her balcony but would not comment on how her son got access to the weapon. Authorities say that is still under investigation.
“I miss my boy. I’m so sorry,” the woman said as she cried and smoked a cigarette.
And in a message to the families of those killed, she said, “I wish I could have done something. I’m sorry for their loss.”
John’s mother told CNN, “He was a good boy,” and there were no warning signs before the shooting unfolded.
Officials said the shooter previously attended special needs classes at Silver Rail but could not confirm whether he had been a student in that particular classroom.
During the pandemic, his mother spoke with CNN affiliate KTVZ about how she hoped the in-person classes for special needs kids will resume. The program is described as being for kids with “intensive behavioral and social skills challenges.”
The mother, who works as a health aide at a local nursing home, had told KTVZ her then 10-year-old son had struggled learning from home and was looking forward to returning to school in 2020.
“I think it will be great for my son to get the help that he needs from the skilled teachers that he needs to get it from,” she told the station.
CNN has reached out to the program for comment.
Additional warrants have been obtained to retrieve data from the devices, a law enforcement source told CNN. Local investigators and the FBI will work to access John’s devices and determine whether there is a trail that leads to the shooting.
Based on the interviews conducted so far, no clear motive has emerged, according to the source.
Meanwhile, the district will begin an investigation into its emergency response procedures, safety planning and other aspects related to the shooting at the school as soon as they are allowed to by law enforcement, Bend-La Pine Schools Superintendent Steven Cook said at a news conference Friday.
Krantz warned uncovering information about the shooter and what led to the attack will take time.
“We may never get that full answer, but we want it,” he said.
CNN’s Nick Watt, Eric Levenson and Norma Galeana contributed to this report.
